          {

          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 337,
            "text": "### 4.2 Sub-action inference (within &#96;memory_action&#96;, &#96;map_action&#96;, etc.)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 338
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 339,
            "text": "Central router or domain router maps entity cues to existing tool args:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 340
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 341,
            "text": "| Cue in entities / text | Sub-action |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 342,
            "text": "|------------------------|------------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 343,
            "text": "| &#96;memory_action&#96; + “remind” | &#96;memory_add&#96; tags=reminder |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 344,
            "text": "| &#96;memory_action&#96; + “what do I have saved” | &#96;memory_search&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 345,
            "text": "| &#96;map_action&#96; + “clear route” | shell &#96;run: reset_route&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 346,
            "text": "| &#96;visual_action&#96; + “3d” | &#96;cspe_open_graph3d&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 347
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 348,
            "text": "Strict mapping tables live in domain routers (config or Python dict), not in OpenAI prompt."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 349
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 350,
            "text": "### 4.3 Legacy tool mapping (migration adapter)"

          {
            "lineNumber": 351
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 352,

            "lineNumber": 353
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 354,
            "text": "| Intent | Adapter tool(s) |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 355,
            "text": "|--------|-----------------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 356,
            "text": "| &#96;route&#96; | &#96;cspe_compute_route&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 357,
            "text": "| &#96;station_search&#96; | &#96;cspe_search_stops&#96; (+ optional &#96;cspe_transport_action&#96; search_map) |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 358,
            "text": "| &#96;station_*&#96; info | &#96;cspe_lookup_place_online&#96; with topic/kind |"

          {

            "text": "| &#96;nearby_stops&#96; | &#96;cspe_nearby_stops&#96; |"

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "lineNumber": 298,
            "text": "Domain routers **select** which service chain runs; they do not duplicate graph/IDFM logic."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 299
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 300,
            "text": "### 3.6 Final response generation"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 301
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 302,
            "text": "**Existing:** &#96;agent_planner&#96; builds &#96;injection_block&#96;; orchestrator sends to Realtime; &#96;normalize_atlas_ui()&#96; for chat UI."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 303
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 304,
            "text": "**Proposed addition — ResponseComposer:**"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 305
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 306,
            "text": "| Input | Execution results + &#96;normalized_intent&#96; + &#96;data_sources_used[]&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 307,
            "text": "| Output | &#96;injection_block&#96; text + optional structured footer (“Shown on map”, “Based on local timetable data…”) |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 308,
            "text": "| Policy | Info-only intents: lead with facts, no UI mention unless &#96;ui_action&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 309,
            "text": "| Policy | Ambiguous resolution: one sentence stating assumption |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 310
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 311,
            "text": "Realtime model remains **answer-only** (no tool calls from model) — same as today."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 312
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 313,
            "text": "---"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 314
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 315,
            "text": "## 4. Proposed Intent Catalog and Execution Triggers"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 316
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 317,
            "text": "### 4.1 Intent → execution mapping"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 318
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 319,
            "text": "| Intent | Domain | Primary execution | &#96;ui_action&#96; default | &#96;response_type&#96; default |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 320,
            "text": "|--------|--------|-------------------|---------------------|-------------------------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 321,
            "text": "| &#96;route&#96; | transport | Resolve origin/destination → &#96;compute_route_from_queries&#96; → shell if UI | true if visual verbs else false | &#96;text_and_ui&#96; or &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 322,
            "text": "| &#96;station_search&#96; | transport | &#96;search_stops&#96; → optional map focus if UI | true if “show/find on map” | per UI rule |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 323,
            "text": "| &#96;station_info&#96; | transport | &#96;lookup_place_for_chat&#96; topic=about/history | false | &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 324,
            "text": "| &#96;station_accessibility&#96; | transport | &#96;lookup_place_for_chat&#96; topic=accessibility → IDFM referential | false | &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 325,
            "text": "| &#96;station_departures&#96; | transport | Local resolve station → IDFM departures / stop_schedules | false | &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 326,
            "text": "| &#96;station_hours&#96; | transport | Local resolve station → IDFM service hours (not POI SerpAPI) | false | &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 327,
            "text": "| &#96;nearby_stops&#96; | transport | &#96;nearby_stops&#96; API; shell if UI | from &#96;ui_action&#96; | &#96;text_and_ui&#96; or &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 328,
            "text": "| &#96;poi_search&#96; | poi | &#96;nearby_pois&#96; with category; shell if UI | from &#96;ui_action&#96; | &#96;text_and_ui&#96; or &#96;text&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 329,
            "text": "| &#96;explore_area&#96; | poi | &#96;explore_area&#96; (stops+POIs or POI-only variant); shell if UI | true if explore/show map | &#96;text_and_ui&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 330,
            "text": "| &#96;map_action&#96; | map_ui | &#96;cspe_transport_action&#96; / shell kinds (refresh, clear, mode) | true | &#96;ui&#96; |"
          }
        ],
        "range": {
          "endPosition": {
            "line": 330
          },
          "startPosition": {
            "line": 296
          }
        },
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\AGENT_ROUTING_ARCHITECTURE_PLAN.md",

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
LCC and show_transfers lack visible UI buttons in TransportMode. They are backend routing options the agent can set. Users may not see buttons for these.

The agent can control most UI buttons through chat commands. It can switch visualizations, graph layers, and modes. It can refresh the map, compute routes, and toggle the search dock. Map focus mode is keyboard-only and inaccessible to the agent. VR graph opening is supported.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

**Short answer: mostly yes for the main transport UI, but not literally every button — and not always reliably from casual chat.**

### What you can ask in chat and it should work
The agent has tools wired to the transport shell, so natural requests like these are in scope:

- **Network layer:** metro, rail, tram, bus, all, other  
- **Map view:** Geographic → 3D map → **3D/VR graph** (opens GraphXR)  
- **Graph layer:** Stops / Stations / Both  
- **Route & search:** fill start/end, compute a route, clear route, switch Route vs Search dock  
- **Map actions:** refresh map, clear UI, reset route, clear highlights  
- **Exploration / POIs / hours / departures** (separate tools, not “buttons” but chat-driven)

Phrasing helps: e.g. “switch to bus mode”, “show the 3D VR graph”, “use station view”, “clear the route”.

### What is **not** fully chat-controlled
- **Immersive VR inside GraphXR** (headset / “Start VR session” in the viewer) — chat can open the **3D/VR graph panel**, not click VR inside the iframe.  
- **Map focus mode** (hide side panels / focus map — keyboard shortcut) — no agent hook.  
- **Picking from autocomplete lists** — agent can type into search fields; choosing a specific suggestion row is weaker than clicking.  
- **Old app modes** (music, memory, etc.) — removed; only transport remains.

### Reliability (important)
It’s **not guaranteed** on every wording. Some commands have hard shortcuts (open 3D graph, clear/reset map); others depend on the planner understanding and calling `cspe_transport_action` with the right fields. Clear, explicit requests work best.

**Bottom line:** You can use chat as a remote control for **most** of the transport UI (modes, viz, layers, route/search, map cleanup). You **cannot** yet drive **everything** — especially **in-viewer VR** and **focus/hide-chrome** — and success varies with how you phrase the request.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
A shared helper function `parse_transport_ui_settings` should be created to parse UI settings into a dictionary. It will return optional fields such as graph_mode, viz, and graph_viz. This helper could live in a new file or be added to intent_fallback.py.

UI settings will be checked before OpenAI calls in intent_pipeline.py and intent_fallback.py. The central intent router will remap route intents to transport actions when graph mode switches are detected. Route transport will use empty origins and destinations as a fallback. Graph mode shortcuts will be added to planner_shortcuts.py. Intent extractor rules and tests for switching modes will also be included.

The parser will detect graph mode switches by matching phrases like "switch to rail mode" against a list of six modes: all, metro, rail, tram, bus, and other. It uses regex to catch variations with or without the word "mode".

Viz switches will detect "geographic" maps, "network_3d" views, and "graph3d" immersive modes. A separate parser will handle graph_viz toggles for stops, stations, or both.

The parser will live in `intent_ui_control.py` as `try_ui_settings_intent`. It returns a `StructuredIntent` for `map_ui` with `entities.mode` set to the detected graph mode. This lets `route_map_ui` handle graph mode switches directly instead of routing through OpenAI.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

You were right — that log shows the bug clearly.

**What happened:** “switch to rail mode” was misread as a **route request** with `mode: rail` but **empty from/to**, so it called `cspe_compute_route` instead of updating the UI. Atlas then answered in text only; the rail button never changed.

**What we fixed:** UI-only commands like that are now detected **before** the intent model runs and routed to `cspe_transport_action` with `graph_mode: rail` and `run: none` (settings change only, no route).

Same path now covers things like:
- “switch to metro / bus / tram mode”
- “switch to geographic / 3D map / 3D VR graph”
- “switch to stops / stations view” (when it’s clearly a layer change, not “stops around X”)

There’s also a safety net if the model still labels it as a route with no endpoints.

**Try again after restarting Atlas** (restart `run_web_app.ps1` or the process on 5055). Then say e.g. “switch to rail mode” — you should see the rail layer button activate without a route compute.

---

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Planning to define simple UI acknowledgment steps. When all successful steps are UI-only, the turn result will use a one-word language-specific fallback summary instead of a full response. Now examining the orchestrator.

The "direct" status still routes to the model unless a test flag is present. The fix belongs in the orchestrator's `route_and_handle`: when a simple UI-only plan succeeds, the system should speak the done summary locally and return True without invoking the model.

Reconsidering the orchestrator fix. A simpler alternative is to have the agent planner return status="direct" with a one-word fallback summary and empty injection for simple UI tasks. The orchestrator would then handle that directly.

Realized that returning a done summary with an empty injection block still routes to the model, because the orchestrator automatically injects AGENT_PLAN_RESULTS when no injection exists. Two fixes are being weighed: introducing a new "local_done" status, or handling simple UI-only completions directly in the orchestrator by speaking the done message and returning True without model invocation.

Settled on a minimal change inside `_done_turn_result`. A helper will detect simple UI-only completions. The planner will return a one-word fallback summary in the final summary field. This avoids adding a new orchestrator status or flag.

The orchestrator's "direct" path will be updated to speak short summaries locally when the injection block is empty. Simple UI-only completions will return status "direct" with an empty injection block and a one-word fallback summary.

Identifying specific simple UI tools for the acknowledgment list. These include mode switches, transport graph mode, and reset or clear actions. A helper function will check each step to confirm it is a successful, settings-only operation.

The helper functions are now defined. `_is_simple_ui_ack_step` accepts mode switches, transport options, and specific `cspe_transport_action` runs such as `none`, `reset_route`, `clear_transport_ui`, `refresh_map`, and `clear_map_highlight`. `_is_simple_ui_ack_turn` checks that every step in the turn qualifies as simple UI-only.

The fallback summary will be a one-word phrase like "Done" or "Terminé." The tool executor's internal summary for `cspe_transport_action` will be overridden by the planner's local response.

Legacy router receipts will also use the one-word fallback for settings-only transport actions. The minimal fix targets two files: `agent_planner.py` for the new helpers and `_done_turn_result` logic, and `orchestrator.py` to speak local summaries directly when no injection is present.

Also updating `orchestrator_tool_utils.py` so `build_local_confirmation` uses the one-word fallback for simple UI tools. The orchestrator will handle `status="done"` turns the same way when the injection block is empty and the final summary is already a short fallback. No extra language detection flag is needed; the existing fallback already covers both English and French.

The orchestrator's "direct" branch currently returns False to the model. It will be updated to return True when the injection block is empty and a final summary is present. The assistant text will be set, the summary spoken via TTS, and the router context updated before returning.</details></think>

Simple UI acknowledgments will return a direct done_fallback status with empty injection. Local confirmation summaries will be replaced by done_fallback when all receipts are simple UI tools.

The helper function checks receipt status and tool name against predefined sets. It also inspects the cspe_transport_action run field to identify simple UI acknowledgments.

A planner-level helper will detect simple UI acknowledgments before execution. It checks the step receipt status and tool name against the predefined sets. For cspe_transport_action, it reads the run value from step arguments or receipt data.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Here’s a quick pass over **each file in the project root** (not folders):

| File | Safe to delete for *running* the app? | Notes |
|------|----------------------------------------|--------|
| **`.env`** | **No — breaks things** | API keys (Mapbox, Azure, OpenAI, IDFM, etc.). `run_web_app.ps1` loads it. Without it, maps/chat/voice fail. |
| **`.gitignore`** | Yes | Git only. No effect on running the app. |
| **`run_web_app.ps1`** | **No — breaks startup** | Main way you start Atlas + API + GraphXR + Vite. |
| **`run_product_shell.ps1`** | Yes *if* you always use `run_web_app.ps1` | Starts only the FastAPI shell on 8787. Handy alternate, not required if you use the full script. |
| **`stop_product_shell.ps1`** | **No if you use `run_web_app.ps1`** | That script calls it before starting the API. |
| **`setup_venv.ps1`** | Yes for daily run | One-time / occasional venv setup. Delete only if you’ll never recreate `.venv`. |
| **`requirements.txt`** | Yes for daily run | Needed to **install** Python deps, not loaded at runtime. Keep if you reinstall the venv. |
| **`build_data_layers.py`** | Yes for daily run | Offline: builds normalized map/POI data under `data/`. Only needed when **regenerating** datasets. |
| **`build_geometry_layers.py`** | Yes for daily run | Same — offline geometry/graph prep. Not used by `run_web_app.ps1`. |
| **`debug.py`** | Yes | Small one-off script to inspect IDFM geojson. Not used by the product. |
| **`_mf_out.txt`** | Yes | Leftover debug log (modulefinder traceback). Trash. |

**Bottom line:** For normal use, keep **`.env`**, **`run_web_app.ps1`**, and **`stop_product_shell.ps1`**. Everything else at root is either setup, offline data tooling, or junk you can remove without stopping the app — as long as **`data/`** is already built and **`.venv`** already exists.

          },

            "text": "    G = te.graph_for(search_mode, search_lcc)"

            "text": "    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []"

            "text": "    for sid, (lon, lat) in idx.station_centroid.items():"

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Station lines are straight chords between centroids. They do not follow actual path geometry. This explains why the simplified station points sit off the drawn edges.

The base network and station overlay render simultaneously. The base network shows real track geometries. The station overlay draws straight chord lines between centroids. Both layers are visible at once. This creates the visual mismatch.

The fix is to use the representative stop instead of the centroid. That main platform stop lies directly on the detailed track geometry. The dot then sits on the actual line rather than floating above it.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Yes — your memory is right.

**What the dots are**  
Multiple platform stops are merged into one logical station (GTFS parent, transfers, same name nearby). The map marker is the **average (centroid)** of those stop coordinates — not a point on the track.

**Why it looks wrong when zooming**  
The map is drawing **two different geometries at once**:

1. **Lines** — real stop-to-stop track geometry (base network, or the orange route path).
2. **Station dots** — centroid positions, often offset from the line when platforms are spread out (long station, separate platforms, transfer hub).

In **hybrid** mode this is most obvious: track-following lines underneath, centroid dots on top.

In **station** mode with a route, the detailed path still follows stops on the rails, but station markers stay at centroids — so dots sit beside the line when you zoom in.

Station-to-station overlay lines are also **straight chords between centroids**, not the actual rail shape, which adds to the mismatch.

**How to fix (conceptually)**  
Pick one visual model and stick to it:

- **Snap markers** — place the station dot on the line you’re actually drawing (nearest point on route edge, or a chosen “main” platform stop instead of the average).
- **Align line + dot** — in station view, draw station links using the real stop path between stations (same geometry routing already uses), not straight centroid-to-centroid lines.
- **Separate layers cleanly** — in pure station mode, hide stop-level track lines and show only the station graph (dots + station edges); in hybrid, optionally draw short connectors from centroid to member platforms so the grouping is obvious rather than “floating.”

The cleanest fix for the zoom weirdness is usually **representative stop + path-following station edges**, or **snap centroids onto the visible route geometry** — so points and lines share one coordinate system.

---

do a chosen “main” platform stop instead of the average

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Implementing `_pick_main_platform_stop` to select the main platform stop. The preferred choice is the GTFS parent stop if it is present in the members list and has coordinates.

If no valid GTFS parent exists, the fallback order is highest degree on non-transfer edges, then total degree, then lexicographic sort by stop_id. Also verifying whether the parent node can be synthetic and missing from the graph.

The existing `station_centroid` field will hold the main platform stop coordinates to avoid renaming it across many files. The `_pick_main_platform_stop` helper will return the selected stop ID or None. For the GTFS parent heuristic, the parent is identified as the member referenced by another member's `parent_map`.</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
I'll modify station_layer.py to pick a single main platform stop instead of averaging. A new `_pick_main_platform_stop` function will handle the selection.

Helper functions are being added to identify transfer edges and compute ride degree and total degree for each stop.

A helper counts how many children in the group point to each parent GTFS ID. The parent with the most children wins, with ties broken by ID. This will guide the main platform stop selection.

The selection logic falls back to the first coordinate-bearing stop if no parent is found. Otherwise it sorts candidates by descending ride degree, then total degree, then ID, and picks the top result. Using `max` with positive degrees would be clearer than `min` with negative ones.

Sorting candidates by descending ride degree, total degree, and ID is simpler than using `max`. The first item in the sorted list resolves ties.</details></think>

import networkx as nx
from src.core.station_layer import build_station_layer, _pick_main_platform_stop

G = nx.Graph()
# Two platforms + parent: parent has fewer ride edges but should win
G.add_node('parent', lon=2.3, lat=48.8, stop_name='Gare')
G.add_node('plat_a', lon=2.301, lat=48.801, stop_name='Gare')
G.add_node('plat_b', lon=2.299, lat=48.799, stop_name='Gare')
G.add_edge('plat_a', 'plat_b', edge_kind='transfer', mode='transfer')
G.add_edge('plat_a', 'n1', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G.add_edge('plat_a', 'n2', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G.add_edge('plat_b', 'n3', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G.add_node('n1', lon=2.31, lat=48.81, stop_name='N1')
G.add_node('n2', lon=2.32, lat=48.82, stop_name='N2')
G.add_node('n3', lon=2.28, lat=48.79, stop_name='N3')

parent_map = {'plat_a': 'parent', 'plat_b': 'parent'}
members = ['parent', 'plat_a', 'plat_b']
main = _pick_main_platform_stop(G, members, parent_map)
assert main == 'parent', main

# No parent in group: pick highest ride degree
G2 = nx.Graph()
G2.add_node('a', lon=1.0, lat=2.0, stop_name='X')
G2.add_node('b', lon=1.001, lat=2.001, stop_name='X')
G2.add_edge('a', 'b', edge_kind='transfer', mode='transfer')
G2.add_edge('a', 'x1', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G2.add_edge('b', 'x2', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G2.add_edge('b', 'x3', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G2.add_node('x1', lon=1.1, lat=2.1, stop_name='Y')
G2.add_node('x2', lon=1.2, lat=2.2, stop_name='Z')
G2.add_node('x3', lon=1.3, lat=2.3, stop_name='W')
main2 = _pick_main_platform_stop(G2, ['a', 'b'], {})
assert main2 == 'b', main2

idx = build_station_layer(G2, project_root='.')
st_id = idx.stop_to_station['a']
lon, lat = idx.station_centroid[st_id]
assert (lon, lat) == (1.001, 2.001), (lon, lat)
print('ok')

import networkx as nx
from src.core.station_layer import build_station_layer, _pick_main_platform_stop

G = nx.Graph()
G.add_node('parent', lon=2.3, lat=48.8, stop_name='Gare')
G.add_node('plat_a', lon=2.301, lat=48.801, stop_name='Gare')
G.add_node('plat_b', lon=2.299, lat=48.799, stop_name='Gare')
G.add_edge('plat_a', 'plat_b', edge_kind='transfer', mode='transfer')
G.add_edge('plat_a', 'n1', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G.add_edge('plat_a', 'n2', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G.add_edge('plat_b', 'n3', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G.add_node('n1', lon=2.31, lat=48.81, stop_name='N1')
G.add_node('n2', lon=2.32, lat=48.82, stop_name='N2')
G.add_node('n3', lon=2.28, lat=48.79, stop_name='N3')

parent_map = {'plat_a': 'parent', 'plat_b': 'parent'}
members = ['parent', 'plat_a', 'plat_b']
main = _pick_main_platform_stop(G, members, parent_map)
assert main == 'parent', main

G2 = nx.Graph()
G2.add_node('a', lon=1.0, lat=2.0, stop_name='X')
G2.add_node('b', lon=1.001, lat=2.001, stop_name='X')
G2.add_edge('a', 'b', edge_kind='transfer', mode='transfer')
G2.add_edge('a', 'x1', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G2.add_edge('b', 'x2', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G2.add_edge('b', 'x3', edge_kind='ride', mode='metro')
G2.add_node('x1', lon=1.1, lat=2.1, stop_name='Y')
G2.add_node('x2', lon=1.2, lat=2.2, stop_name='Z')
G2.add_node('x3', lon=1.3, lat=2.3, stop_name='W')
main2 = _pick_main_platform_stop(G2, ['a', 'b'], {})
assert main2 == 'b', main2

idx = build_station_layer(G2, project_root='.')
st_id = idx.stop_to_station['a']
lon, lat = idx.station_centroid[st_id]
assert (lon, lat) == (1.001, 2.001), (lon, lat)
print('ok')

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Done. Station map markers now use a **main platform stop** instead of the average of all platforms.

**Selection order:**
1. **GTFS parent stop** — if the group has a parent station in GTFS, that stop’s coordinates are used.
2. **Most connected platform** — otherwise the stop with the most non-transfer (ride) edges.
3. **Stable tie-break** — highest total degree, then lowest stop id.

The field is still named `station_centroid` internally, but it now holds the main platform’s lon/lat, so dots should sit on the drawn lines much more often when zooming.

**Restart** `run_web_app.ps1` so the cached station layer reloads. If a map still looks old, clear the route or refresh — map HTML can be disk-cached for static views.

          {
            "lineNumber": 35,
            "text": "_ROUTER_SYSTEM = \"\"\"You are a strict routing function inside a voice assistant."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 36,
            "text": "Your ONLY job is to output a single JSON object (no extra text) describing what to do next."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 37
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 38,
            "text": "You must choose EXACTLY ONE:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 39,
            "text": "1) DIRECT answer (no tool)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 40,
            "text": "2) TOOL call (choose ONE tool and its args)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 41
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 42,
            "text": "NON-REFUSAL:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 43,
            "text": "- Never refuse because of capability. If the user asks for something that requires a tool, choose the closest tool."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 44
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 45,
            "text": "OUTPUT JSON SCHEMA:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 46,
            "text": "{"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 47,
            "text": "  \"mode\": \"direct\" | \"tool\","
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 48,
            "text": "  \"tool_name\": string | null,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 49,
            "text": "  \"args\": object | null,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 50,
            "text": "  \"topic\": string,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 51,
            "text": "  \"confidence\": number,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 52,
            "text": "  \"needs_clarification\": boolean,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 53,
            "text": "  \"clarifying_question\": string,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 54,
            "text": "  \"reason\": string"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 55,
            "text": "}"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 56
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 57,
            "text": "RULES:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 58,
            "text": "- If mode=\"direct\": tool_name=null, args=null."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 59,
            "text": "- If mode=\"tool\": tool_name is one of the allowed tools; args is an object."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 60,
            "text": "- Keep args minimal: include required fields; include optional fields only if the user asked for them."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 61,
            "text": "- Resolve references using CONTEXT (e.g., it/that/them/these/those) to a concrete topic/entity."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 62,
            "text": "- If CONTEXT includes LAST_PLACE or a recent station/POI lookup, treat topic-only follow-ups (\"what are the working hours\", \"is it accessible\", \"any disruptions\") as about that same place — do not ask the user to repeat the name."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 63,
            "text": "- PARIS / ÎLE-DE-FRANCE TRANSIT (CSPE graph): For stop/station lookup, metro/RER/tram/bus routes between stops in the CSPE dataset, or graph connectivity, use cspe_search_stops and/or cspe_route. Prefer these for pure routing in the graph. When the user asks in chat about a station or POI (info, history, hours, accessibility, disruptions, reviews), always use cspe_lookup_place_online with the right topic — never cspe_show_station_or_line_info for those questions. Do not ask which API or data source to use."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 64,
            "text": "- If the request is ambiguous or missing a required argument for the chosen tool, set needs_clarification=true and ask ONE short question."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 65,
            "text": "- clarifying_question must be in the same language as the user (English or French only)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 66,
            "text": "- topic: a short canonical subject of the user's request (used by the system to handle follow-ups)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 67,
            "text": "- reason: a short phrase for debugging (not a chain-of-thought)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 68,
            "text": "\"\"\""
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 69
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 70,
            "text": "# Reuse a single client instance for connection pooling / lower overhead."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 71,
            "text": "_CLIENT = OpenAI()"
          }

          },

          {

            "text": "    )"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 165
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 166,
            "text": "    # Prefer structured JSON output if supported; fall back to plain text."
          },
          {

          {

            "text": "        temperature=0,"
          },
          {

            "text": "        response_format={\"type\": \"json_object\"},"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 175,
            "text": "        max_tokens=220,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 176,
            "text": "    )"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 177
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 178,
            "text": "    content = (resp.choices[0].message.content or \"\").strip()"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 179,
            "text": "    obj = _safe_json_load(content)"

          {

          },

          },
          {

          },

          {
            "lineNumber": 107,
            "text": "_PLANNER_SYSTEM = \"\"\"You are Atlas Planner for CSPE (transport, POI, map, 3D graph)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 108
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 109,
            "text": "Output ONE JSON object only (no markdown). Use strict tool names from ALLOWED TOOLS."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 110
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 111,
            "text": "SCHEMA:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 112,
            "text": "{"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 113,
            "text": "  \"status\": \"continue\" | \"done\" | \"clarify\" | \"direct\","
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 114,
            "text": "  \"steps\": [{\"tool\": \"tool_name\", \"arguments\": {}, \"reason\": \"optional\"}],"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 115,
            "text": "  \"tool_name\": null,"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 116,
            "text": "  \"args\": {},"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 117,
            "text": "  \"clarifying_question\": \"\","
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 118,
            "text": "  \"final_summary\": \"\","
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 119,
            "text": "  \"topic\": \"\""
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 120,
            "text": "}"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 121
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 122,
            "text": "RULES:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 123,
            "text": "- Natural-language commands: choose the minimal valid tool chain in \"steps\" (ordered)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 124,
            "text": "- Do NOT invent tools, routes, stop names, or UI state — only fill arguments you can infer."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 125,
            "text": "- Call cspe_get_current_context when you need current mode, map, routing scope, or graph session."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 126,
            "text": "- Routes: use cspe_compute_route with from_query, to_query, sync_ui:true (not cspe_route)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 127,
            "text": "- Stop lookup: cspe_search_stops with query (tool name is cspe_search_stops, not cspe_search_stop)."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 128,
            "text": "- Area exploration: cspe_nearby_stops, cspe_nearby_pois, cspe_explore_area (radius_m, categories, sync_ui). Use cspe_get_current_context for \"this station\" / \"near here\". Never use cspe_lookup_place_online or status=direct when the user wants POIs/stops shown on the map."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 129,
            "text": "- Filter displayed results: cspe_filter_visible_results after an exploration step."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 130,
            "text": "- Map UI patches: cspe_update_map or cspe_transport_action — never assume results."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 131,
            "text": "- Graph layer only (metro/rail/tram/bus/all): cspe_transport_action with spec run=none and graph_mode — NOT cspe_compute_route."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 132,
            "text": "- Visualization only (geographic / network_3d / graph3d): cspe_transport_action with spec viz and run=none."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 133,
            "text": "- Follow-ups: if CONTEXT or WORLD_STATE names a place/station from the previous turn, reuse it when the user asks a topic-only follow-up (e.g. \"what are the working hours\", \"is it accessible\") without repeating the place name."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 134,
            "text": "- status=clarify when required args are missing; status=direct only for pure Q\u0026A with no tools."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 135,
            "text": "- Never refuse; pick the closest valid plan or ask one clarifying question."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 136,
            "text": "- User-facing text (clarifying_question, final_summary) must match the user's language: English or French only."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 137,
            "text": "\"\"\""
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 138
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 139
          },

            "isSignature": true,

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
I'll explain the OpenAI agent decision flow in two stages, then cover the IDFM API implementation.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Here is the short version of both pieces.

## How the OpenAI agent decides

It is **two steps**, not “the model picks a tool directly.”

**1. Understand intent (OpenAI)**  
Your message goes to an **intent extractor** (`extract_intent_openai`). It returns structured JSON only:

- **domain** — transport, POI, map UI, 3D graph, general chat  
- **intent** — route, station departures, POI search, map action, etc.  
- **entities** — station name, origin/destination, line, mode  
- **ui_action** — should the map/UI change?

It does **not** choose which tool to run. Some phrases are handled **before** OpenAI (e.g. “switch to rail mode”).

**2. Route to tools (deterministic code)**  
That JSON goes through a **central router** → **domain routers** (`transport`, `poi`, `map_ui`, …). Those are plain rules, for example:

- route A → B → `cspe_compute_route` (local graph)  
- station departures → `cspe_lookup_place_online` (local resolve + IDFM)  
- show on map → add a UI sync step  
- pure chat → no tool, model answers directly  

**3. Execute and respond**  
The planner runs those `cspe_*` tools (HTTP calls to the product shell on port 8787). Results are injected back into the voice/chat model so it can answer in natural language. Simple UI actions can skip that and just say “Done.”

**Split of responsibility**

| Layer | Who decides |
|--------|-------------|
| What the user wants | OpenAI intent JSON |
| Which tool(s) to run | Fixed routing rules |
| Routes, stops, map geometry | Local CSPE graph |
| Live station info | IDFM (see below) |

---

## How IDFM is implemented

IDFM is **enrichment only** — not routing, not POI search.

**When it runs**  
Only after a station is **already found in the local graph** (e.g. “next departures at Châtelet”). Flow:

`cspe_lookup_place_online` → local station match → `enrich_local_station()`

**Two data sources**

1. **Live PRIM Navitia API** (`idfm_client.py`)  
   - Base: `prim.iledefrance-mobilites.fr/marketplace/v2/navitia`  
   - Auth: `IDFM_API_KEY` in `.env`  
   - Maps your stop ids (`IDFM:22006`) → Navitia `stop_point:IDFM:…`  
   - Then calls endpoints for stop area, lines, modes, **departures**, schedules, disruptions  

2. **Cached referential CSVs** (`idfm_referential.py`)  
   - Downloaded from Île-de-France Mobilités open data (arrets, accessibility)  
   - Cached under `data/derived/idfm/` for ~24h  
   - Used mainly for **accessibility** labels  

**What comes back**  
A text summary (`idfm_summary`) plus structured data (lines, modes, departures, hours, accessibility, alerts). The agent uses that to answer; if the key is missing or the API fails, it falls back to local graph info only.

**Important constraint**  
IDFM never does open-ended “find this place.” The station must exist locally first; IDFM adds live/official detail on top.

Hi, I want to test the VR/WebXR part of this project on my Meta Quest 3.

Please analyze the project structure and the current implementation first, especially everything related to:

* frontend VR/WebXR integration,
* Babylon.js scene setup,

* environment variables,
* HTTPS / local network requirements,

Before giving me the final steps, answer these questions clearly:

1. What frontend command should I run to start the project?
2. What backend services are required for the VR mode to work?
3. Does the VR mode work only after creating/loading a graph project, or can it be tested with a demo scene?
4. Which exact URL should I open from the Meta Quest 3 browser?
5. Does WebXR require HTTPS in this project, and if yes, what is the simplest way to run it locally with HTTPS?
6. Can the Quest access the dev server directly through my local network? If yes, what IP/port should be used?
7. Are there any CORS, firewall, host binding, or Vite/Next.js config changes needed so the Quest can access the app?
8. Where in the code is the VR mode initialized?
9. Which buttons/controllers are already implemented for VR interactions?
10. What is the minimal test scenario to confirm that VR is working correctly?

After answering these, give me a step-by-step guide written for a beginner, assuming I have:

* my PC running the project,
* my Meta Quest 3 connected to the same Wi-Fi network,

The guide should be practical and direct:

* commands to run,
* files to check or modify,
* how to get my PC local IP,
* how to open the app inside the Quest browser,
* how to enter VR mode,
* how to verify that controllers, selection, movement, and graph rendering work,
* common errors and how to fix them.

Do not rewrite the whole project. Focus only on what is necessary to test the VR part on a real Meta Quest 3.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The Quest VR viewer URL follows this pattern: `http://LAN_IP:3000/viewer?session=XXX&api=http://LAN_IP:8787&sync=...&embedded=1`. This address must be reachable from the Quest over the same local network.

Two ways to reach the Quest:

- **Path A**: Open the main app at `http://LAN_IP:5173` and navigate to the 3D viewer. Set `VITE_API_BASE` and `VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL` to the LAN IP in `.env` before starting. Otherwise the iframe defaults to `127.0.0.1:8787`.
- **Path B**: Open the GraphXR viewer URL directly. Create a session on the PC first so the Quest can fetch it.

The Quest 3 standalone browser requires HTTPS for WebXR. Plain HTTP on a LAN IP will not allow entering immersive mode. Use ngrok to tunnel ports 3000 and 8787. Alternatively generate a local certificate with mkcert and serve through a reverse proxy such as Caddy or nginx. Next.js 13+ supports experimental HTTPS via `next dev --experimental-https`. Air Link or Meta Quest Link from a PC browser will not help because the Quest itself needs a secure context.

A self-signed certificate on the LAN will likely require the user to manually accept it inside the Quest browser before WebXR loads. For ngrok specifically, the free tier allows only one public tunnel at a time, so the viewer and API must either use separate tunnels or route through a single tunnel with custom paths. Cloudflare Tunnel or localtunnel are viable alternatives.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

## Project structure (VR-relevant parts)

| Part | Role |
|------|------|
| `frontend/` (Vite, port **5173**) | Main CSPE UI; Transport mode has the **3D/VR graph** button |
| `viewers/graphxr/` (Next.js, port **3000**) | Babylon.js 3D + WebXR viewer |
| `backend/product_shell/` (FastAPI, port **8787**) | Builds graph sessions via `/api/transport/graph3d/*` |
| `run_web_app.ps1` | Starts all of the above together |

VR is **not** in the main Vite app. It lives in **GraphXR**, embedded as an iframe after the backend creates a graph session.

There is **no standalone VR demo scene**. You need a valid `session` + `api` URL params (created when you open **3D/VR graph** in Transport mode).

---

## Answers to your 10 questions

### 1. What frontend command should I run?

**Recommended (starts everything):**

```powershell
cd C:\Users\LEGION\Desktop\CSPE
.\run_web_app.ps1
```

This starts API (8787), GraphXR (3000), and Vite (5173).

**Manual (only if debugging):**

```powershell
# Terminal 1 — backend (must be running first)
python -m uvicorn backend.product_shell.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8787

# Terminal 2 — GraphXR viewer
cd viewers\graphxr
npm install
npm run dev -- -p 3000 -H 0.0.0.0

# Terminal 3 — main frontend
cd frontend
npm run dev
```

---

### 2. What backend services are required for VR?

| Service | Port | Required? |
|---------|------|-----------|
| **Product shell API** | **8787** | **Yes** — creates/serves graph sessions |
| **GraphXR viewer** | **3000** | **Yes** — renders 3D/VR |
| **Vite frontend** | **5173** | **Yes** (easiest path) — button that opens the viewer |
| Atlas API | 5055 | **No** for manual VR testing |

Graph data comes from `data/derived/routing/graph_bundle.pkl` (built automatically on first use from GTFS data).

---

### 3. Demo scene or loaded project?

**No demo scene.** You must load a graph session from CSPE.

- A **route is optional** — the full transport graph still loads.
- You **do not** need to compute a route first; clicking **3D/VR graph** in Transport mode is enough.
- Opening `http://…:3000/viewer` alone shows: *“Open this viewer from CSPE after computing a transport route.”*

---

### 4. Which exact URL on Meta Quest 3?

**Easiest path (main app):**

```text
http://YOUR_PC_LAN_IP:5173
```

Then: **Transport** → **3D/VR graph** → **VR** button inside the viewer.

**Direct viewer URL (only if you already have a session id):**

```text
http://YOUR_PC_LAN_IP:3000/viewer?session=SESSION_ID&api=http://YOUR_PC_LAN_IP:8787&embedded=1
```

Replace `YOUR_PC_LAN_IP` (e.g. `192.168.1.42`) and `SESSION_ID`.

---

### 5. Does WebXR require HTTPS?

**Yes, for Quest over Wi‑Fi.**

- Desktop `http://127.0.0.1` can work for local WebXR testing.
- Quest browser on `http://192.168.x.x` is **not** a secure context → **WebXR/VR will fail** on plain HTTP.

**Simplest options for Quest:**

1. **ngrok** (beginner-friendly) — HTTPS tunnels to your PC  
2. **Next.js dev HTTPS** — `npm run dev -- -p 3000 -H 0.0.0.0 --experimental-https` (self-signed; accept cert on Quest)  
3. **mkcert + reverse proxy** — more setup, good long-term

The repo does **not** ship HTTPS out of the box.

---

### 6. Can Quest access the dev server on LAN?

**Yes**, if:

- PC and Quest are on the **same Wi‑Fi**
- Windows Firewall allows ports **5173**, **3000**, **8787**
- Servers bind to **0.0.0.0** (already configured)

**Get your PC IP (PowerShell):**

```powershell
ipconfig
```

Use the **IPv4 Address** under your Wi‑Fi adapter (e.g. `192.168.1.42`).

| What | URL |
|------|-----|
| Main app | `http://192.168.1.42:5173` |
| GraphXR | `http://192.168.1.42:3000/viewer` |
| API | `http://192.168.1.42:8787` |

---

### 7. CORS / firewall / config changes for Quest?

**Before starting**, add to repo-root `.env`:

```env
VITE_API_BASE=http://YOUR_PC_LAN_IP:8787
VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL=http://YOUR_PC_LAN_IP:3000/viewer
```

Why: default URLs use `127.0.0.1`, which on Quest means **the headset itself**, not your PC.

**CORS:** FastAPI already allows LAN origins via regex in `backend/product_shell/main.py` (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x). Usually no change needed.

**Firewall:** Allow inbound on **5173**, **3000**, **8787** for private networks, or temporarily disable firewall to test.

**Vite/Next:** Already bind `0.0.0.0`. No extra config unless you add HTTPS.

---

### 8. Where is VR mode initialized?

| Step | File | What happens |
|------|------|----------------|
| Toggle VR UI | `viewers/graphxr/app/viewer/ViewerClient.tsx` | `isVRMode` state; **VR** button sets it |
| VR scene mount | Same file | `isVRMode ? <GraphSceneXR /> : <GraphSceneWeb />` |
| WebXR init | `viewers/graphxr/app/components/3DandXRComponents/Graph/GraphSceneXR.tsx` | `createDefaultXRExperienceAsync({ sessionMode: 'immersive-vr' })` |
| VR button UI | `viewers/graphxr/app/components/3DandXRComponents/UI/OverlayControls.tsx` | **VR** button |

Flow: **3D/VR graph** (CSPE) → graph loads → click **VR** → Babylon starts WebXR → browser/headset **Enter VR** prompt.

---

### 9. Which controllers/interactions are implemented?

Oculus Touch (Quest 3) in `GraphSceneXR.tsx` + `GraphRenderer.ts`:

| Input | Action |
|-------|--------|
| **Thumbsticks** | Free-fly move + rotate |
| **Trigger** | Select node/edge |
| **Grip (squeeze)** | Grab/release entire graph |
| **A / X** | Toggle in-headset VR menu |
| **Hover** | Highlight + tooltip |

In-headset HUD shows: *Grip: grab world · Sticks: fly/rotate · A/X: menu · Trigger: select*

VR menu supports filters, labels, reset filters. Layout changes from VR menu are **not** implemented (desktop only).

---

### 10. Minimal test to confirm VR works

1. PC: run `.\run_web_app.ps1` with `.env` LAN URLs set.
2. PC browser: open `http://127.0.0.1:5173` → Transport → **3D/VR graph** → see 3D nodes/edges.
3. Click **VR** → on PC, use browser WebXR or continue on Quest with HTTPS.
4. Enter immersive mode → see graph in headset.
5. **Thumbsticks** → move/turn.
6. **Trigger** on a node → selection/details.
7. **Grip** → graph moves with controller.
8. **A/X** → VR menu appears.

Success = graph visible in headset + movement + trigger selection work.

---

## Known limitations

- **No offline VR demo** — needs backend session.
- **HTTPS required on Quest** — plain LAN HTTP loads the page but VR entry often fails.
- **Large graphs** (`bus`, `all`) can be slow; start with **metro**.
- **Sessions expire** after ~30 minutes.
- **No Docker** setup in repo.
- **`webxr-polyfill`** is installed but unused.
- Atlas/voice is optional for this test.

---

## Step-by-step guide (beginner, Quest 3)

### Step 0 — Prerequisites on PC

- Node.js, Python venv, project dependencies installed (as you already use for CSPE).
- Quest 3 and PC on the **same Wi‑Fi**.
- `.env` at repo root with Mapbox etc. as you already have.

### Step 1 — Get your PC IP

```powershell
ipconfig
```

Note Wi‑Fi **IPv4** (example: `192.168.1.42`).

### Step 2 — Edit `.env`

Add or update (use your real IP):

```env
VITE_API_BASE=http://192.168.1.42:8787
VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL=http://192.168.1.42:3000/viewer
```

Save the file **before** starting the app.

### Step 3 — Allow Windows Firewall (once)

PowerShell **as Administrator**:

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "CSPE Vite" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 5173 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "CSPE GraphXR" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 3000 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "CSPE API" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 8787 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow
```

### Step 4 — Start the stack

```powershell
cd C:\Users\LEGION\Desktop\CSPE
.\run_web_app.ps1
```

Wait until you see Vite on `0.0.0.0:5173` and GraphXR on port 3000.

**Quick PC check:**

- `http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/health` → `"transport_graph3d": true`
- `http://127.0.0.1:5173` → app loads

First graph load may take a minute while the bundle builds.

### Step 5 — Test on PC first (recommended)

1. Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173`
2. Go to **Transport**
3. Keep mode **metro** (smaller graph)
4. Click **3D/VR graph**
5. Wait for 3D nodes/edges
6. Click **VR** → if you have a PC VR headset/browser WebXR, test enter VR here

If this fails on PC, fix before using Quest.

### Step 6 — HTTPS for Quest WebXR

**Option A — ngrok (simplest for first test)**

1. Install [ngrok](https://ngrok.com/)
2. Two tunnels (API + viewer):

```powershell
ngrok http 8787
# note HTTPS URL, e.g. https://abc123.ngrok-free.app

ngrok http 3000
# note HTTPS URL, e.g. https://def456.ngrok-free.app
```

3. Update `.env` and restart app:

```env
VITE_API_BASE=https://abc123.ngrok-free.app
VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL=https://def456.ngrok-free.app/viewer
```

4. Restart `.\run_web_app.ps1`

**Option B — Next dev HTTPS (self-signed)**

GraphXR only; you still need HTTPS for API (uvicorn SSL or ngrok for 8787):

```powershell
cd viewers\graphxr
npm run dev -- -p 3000 -H 0.0.0.0 --experimental-https
```

Accept the certificate warning on Quest when prompted.

### Step 7 — Open on Quest 3

1. Put on Quest → open **Browser**
2. Go to:

```text
https://YOUR_HTTPS_OR_LAN_URL:5173
```

(or ngrok HTTPS URL for Vite if you tunnel 5173 too)

3. **Transport** → **3D/VR graph**
4. Wait for the 3D graph in the iframe
5. Tap **VR** (right-side controls in embedded viewer)
6. Tap browser **Enter VR** / immersive button when it appears
7. PC screen may show *“VR Session Active”* — that is normal; the view is in the headset

### Step 8 — Verify in headset

- See colored nodes and edges
- **Thumbsticks** → fly around
- **Trigger** → select a stop/node
- **Grip** → grab and move the whole graph
- **A or X** → open VR menu

### Step 9 — Common errors

| Problem | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Page won’t load on Quest | Wrong IP / firewall | Recheck `ipconfig`, firewall rules, same Wi‑Fi |
| Graph iframe blank / “Missing API” | `127.0.0.1` in URLs | Set `VITE_API_BASE` and `VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL` to PC LAN IP or ngrok HTTPS; restart app |
| “Unable to load 3D/VR graph” / 503 | Graph bundle missing or still building | Wait; check `http://PC_IP:8787/api/health`; ensure GTFS data exists under `data/` |
| 3D works but **VR button does nothing** | HTTP on Quest (no secure context) | Use HTTPS (ngrok or `--experimental-https`) |
| CORS error in viewer | API origin blocked | Ensure Quest opens same host style as in `.env`; CORS regex should allow LAN |
| Session expired | 30 min TTL | Click **3D/VR graph** again to refresh |
| Very slow / crash | Graph too big | Use **metro**, not **all** or **bus** |
| Certificate warning | Self-signed HTTPS | Accept/trust on Quest browser and continue |

---

## Files to check if something breaks

| File | Why |
|------|-----|
| `.env` | `VITE_API_BASE`, `VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL` |
| `run_web_app.ps1` | Ports, auto-start GraphXR |
| `frontend/src/transport/graph3dSync.ts` | How viewer URL is built |
| `viewers/graphxr/app/viewer/ViewerClient.tsx` | Session loading, VR toggle |
| `viewers/graphxr/app/components/3DandXRComponents/Graph/GraphSceneXR.tsx` | WebXR + controllers |
| `backend/product_shell/main.py` | CORS |
| `logs/health.log` | Service startup issues |

---

**Bottom line:** Run `.\run_web_app.ps1`, point `.env` at your PC’s LAN IP (or HTTPS tunnels), open Transport → **3D/VR graph** on Quest, then **VR** → **Enter VR**. Plain HTTP is fine for checking that the 3D graph loads; **HTTPS is required for actual WebXR on Quest 3.**

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Yes — there are controls, but they split into **on-screen buttons** (before/during setup) and **headset controller inputs** (once you’re inside VR).

## On-screen buttons (2D overlay)

These show **before you enter immersive VR** (`!isInXR`). When embedded in CSPE’s Transport view, they appear as a **vertical bar on the right**:

| Button | What it does |
|--------|----------------|
| **Reset** | Resets the camera view |
| **Labels** | Show/hide node labels |
| **Filters** | Opens the filter panel (hide/show nodes & edges) |
| **VR** | Switches from desktop 3D mode to the WebXR-ready scene |

**Not shown in CSPE:** Edit, Export, Share — those exist in the component but are disabled in the embedded viewer.

**When you click a node/edge (desktop 3D):** a **Details** panel pops up (bottom-right) with node/edge info and a close (×) button.

**After you enter VR:** the overlay toolbar **hides**. The PC/phone screen instead shows **“VR Session Active”** and a **Stop VR Session** button (reloads the page).

There is also a **browser/Babylon “Enter VR”** prompt when WebXR starts — that’s what actually puts you in the headset.

---

## Desktop 3D mode (mouse)

Before clicking **VR**:

- **Left drag** — orbit around the graph  
- **Scroll / pinch** — zoom  
- **Right drag** — pan  
- **Click** — select a node or edge (opens Details panel)

---

## Inside VR (Quest controllers)

Once immersive mode is active:

| Control | Action |
|---------|--------|
| **Thumbsticks** | Fly around + rotate |
| **Trigger** | Select node/edge |
| **Grip (squeeze)** | Grab/release the whole graph |
| **A / X** | Open/close the in-headset **VR menu** |

A small **HUD** in the headset lists these commands (Grip, Sticks, A/X, Trigger).

### VR menu (A/X button)

Floating 3D panel in front of you with:

- **Layout buttons** (Frucht-Rein, Kamada-Kawai, sphere, grid, etc.) — **shown but do nothing useful for CSPE** (layout changes aren’t wired for transport graphs)
- **FILTRES…** — opens VR filter panel  
- **RESET FILTRES** — show all nodes again  
- **TOGGLE LABELS** — show/hide labels  
- **FERMER** — close the menu  

Selecting a node in VR can also open a **VR details panel** (neighbors, info, reset filters).

---

## Short answer

- **Yes**, there are on-screen buttons: **Reset, Labels, Filters, VR** (+ Details when you select something).  
- **In VR**, most interaction is **controller-based**, not on-screen buttons — plus the **VR menu** on **A/X**.  
- The only on-screen control while in VR (on the flat browser) is **Stop VR Session**.

---

_**User**_

make the vr/3d open in new tab instead of integrated in our atlas cspe ui

---

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
I'll recommend practical voice-to-text libraries and models for the CSPE project.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

For **this CSPE project**, voice → text is already handled like this:

## What CSPE uses today

| Direction | Service | Model / library |
|-----------|---------|-----------------|
| **Voice → text (STT)** | **OpenAI Realtime API** (Atlas voice session) | **`whisper-1`** for input transcription |
| **Text → voice (TTS)** | **Azure AI Speech** | Your `AZURE_SPEECH_KEY` — **output only**, not transcription |

Flow: you hold the mic in **AtlasRailPanel** → frontend calls `POST /api/atlas/input-mode` with `"voice"` → Atlas opens a Realtime WebSocket → your speech is transcribed with **Whisper** → the planner/agent runs on that text.

You already have **`AZURE_SPEECH_KEY`** in `.env`, but in this project it’s used for **speaking answers**, not for listening.

---

## If you want to add / change STT

**Best fit with your current stack**

1. **Keep OpenAI Realtime + `whisper-1`** — already integrated; good for live voice commands in French/English.
2. **OpenAI `gpt-4o-transcribe` / `whisper-1` API** — if you only need “record audio → get text” (no live session), simpler than Realtime.
3. **Azure Speech-to-Text** — natural if you want one Azure account for both STT and TTS; strong for French.

**Local / offline (no cloud)**

4. **`faster-whisper`** (Python) — very common; runs Whisper locally; good if you don’t want to send audio to the cloud.

**Browser-only (quick experiments)**

5. **Web Speech API** (`webkitSpeechRecognition`) — free, no backend, but less reliable than Whisper/Azure.

---

## Practical recommendation

- **For Atlas voice in CSPE:** stick with **OpenAI Realtime + `whisper-1`** — it’s what the architecture expects.
- **For a simple “transcribe this clip” feature:** **`faster-whisper`** (local) or **OpenAI Whisper API** (cloud).
- **If you want one cloud vendor:** add **Azure Speech STT** alongside your existing Azure TTS key.

If you say whether you mean **live mic in Atlas**, **upload a file**, or **Quest/browser**, I can point to the exact place to wire it in.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Yes. Joystick movement in VR is implemented in **`GraphSceneXR.tsx`**, using **Babylon.js’s built-in WebXR movement feature** — not custom thumbstick polling.

## Where it lives

**File:** `viewers/graphxr/app/components/3DandXRComponents/Graph/GraphSceneXR.tsx`

After WebXR starts (`createDefaultXRExperienceAsync`), locomotion is enabled here:

```256:276:viewers/graphxr/app/components/3DandXRComponents/Graph/GraphSceneXR.tsx
            // 3. Setup Locomotion (Free Fly)
            const featuresManager = xr.baseExperience.featuresManager;
            try {
                const locomotion = featuresManager.enableFeature(
                    WebXRFeatureName.MOVEMENT,
                    'latest',
                    {
                        xrInput: xr.input,
                        movementOrientationFollowsViewerPose: false,
                        movementOrientationFollowsController: true, // Direction follows controller
                        movementSpeed: 0.5, // Reasonable speed
                        rotationSpeed: 0.5,
                        movementEnabled: true,
                        rotationEnabled: true, // Smooth rotation
                        movementThreshold: 0.05
                    }
                );
                console.log('[VR] Free Fly Locomotion enabled');
            } catch (error) {
                console.error('[VR] Error enabling locomotion:', error);
            }
```

## What that means in practice

| Setting | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `WebXRFeatureName.MOVEMENT` | Babylon reads **Quest thumbsticks** and moves the XR camera |
| `movementOrientationFollowsController: true` | Move/turn relative to **controller direction** |
| `movementSpeed: 0.5` | Fly speed |
| `rotationSpeed: 0.5` | Turn speed with stick |
| `disableTeleportation: true` (earlier in file) | **No teleport** — free-fly only |

So on Quest 3: **thumbsticks = fly + rotate** in the headset. Babylon handles the stick input internally.

## Other VR controls (same file)

- **Grip** — grab/move the whole graph (lines 306–329)
- **A/X** — VR menu (lines 282–304)
- **Trigger** — node selection (in `GraphRenderer.ts`)

The in-headset HUD also documents this:

```365:368:viewers/graphxr/app/components/3DandXRComponents/Graph/GraphSceneXR.tsx

                    "Grip: Saisir Monde",
                    "Sticks: Voler/Tourner",
                    "A/X: Menu | Trigger: Select"
```

## Note

`useVRLocomotion.ts` is **empty/deprecated** — the comment says locomotion was moved into `GraphSceneXR.tsx` for Babylon v8.

To change how movement feels, edit **`movementSpeed`**, **`rotationSpeed`**, and the `MOVEMENT` options in that block — there’s no separate custom joystick handler elsewhere.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Yes — that’s basically how Babylon maps it by default on Quest.

Your project doesn’t implement custom stick code; it uses Babylon’s **`WebXRFeatureName.MOVEMENT`**, which uses this default split:

| Controller | Stick | Role |
|------------|-------|------|
| **Left** | Thumbstick **X** (left/right) | **Tourner** — rotate horizontally |
| **Right** | Thumbstick **forward/back** | **Voler** — move forward/back |
| **Right** | Thumbstick **left/right** | **Strafe** — slide sideways |

So it’s not strictly “one stick = only fly, one stick = only turn”:

- **Left stick** → mainly **turn** (left/right).
- **Right stick** → **move** (forward/back + sideways).

The HUD line *“Sticks: Voler/Tourner”* is a short summary of that split.

### Details worth knowing

1. **Movement follows the controller direction** — because your config has `movementOrientationFollowsController: true`, “forward” on the right stick is relative to where you point the **right** controller, not just your head.

2. **“Voler” is horizontal** — movement stays on a flat plane (no up/down with the stick). There’s no vertical fly in this setup.

3. **Left stick up/down** is read by Babylon but **not used** for rotation in the current movement logic — only left/right turn matters.

If you want true up/down flight on a stick, or swap left/right roles, that would need custom stick handling instead of the default `MOVEMENT` feature.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Babylon.js captures left stick vertical movement but does not apply it as pitch rotation. I am evaluating options to implement this.

The best approach is to hook into `scene.onBeforeRenderObservable`, read the left controller thumbstick Y value, and apply it to `xrCamera.cameraRotation.x` with clamping. This mirrors how yaw is currently handled on the Y axis.

WebXRCamera exposes `cameraRotation` as a Vector3 in radians. I will attach the `onBeforeRenderObservable` listener when entering XR, mapping the left stick Y axis to `cameraRotation.x` for pitch control.

I am now writing the implementation. Pitch speed and threshold constants are set. The observer will find the left controller via its handedness and read the motion controller's Y axis.

The code iterates through motion controller components to locate the thumbstick and read its Y axis. It applies a time-based delta multiplied by the speed constant and handedness sign to `cameraRotation.x`.

The observer will clamp `cameraRotation.x` between `MIN_PITCH` and `MAX_PITCH`. I need to import `Scalar` from `@babylonjs/core` for clamping. I am also checking how to access controllers in Babylon 8, since the movement feature uses internal `_controllers` while the custom code can rely on `xr.input.onControllerAddedObservable`.</details></think>

Done. **Left stick now controls look up/down** as well as turn left/right.

### What changed (`GraphSceneXR.tsx`)

Babylon’s built-in movement only uses the **left stick X** for turning. A custom hook was added that reads the **left stick Y** each frame and adjusts **`cameraRotation.x`** (pitch), clamped so you can’t flip upside down.

| Left stick | Action |
|------------|--------|
| **Left / right** | Turn (unchanged — Babylon `MOVEMENT`) |
| **Up / down** | Look up / look down (new) |

| Right stick | Action (unchanged) |
|-------------|---------------------|
| Forward / back + strafe | Fly |

The in-headset HUD now says: **“Gauche: Tourner + Haut/Bas”**.

### Try it

Restart GraphXR (or `run_web_app.ps1`), open 3D/VR, enter VR, and use the **left stick** vertically to pitch the view.

If up/down feels inverted on Quest, say so — it’s a one-line sign flip.

Confirmed `http-proxy` is available in the root `package.json` and `node_modules` exists there for `proxy-vr.js`. Now implementing the full changes to `run_web_app.ps1`.

Adding helper functions to `run_web_app.ps1` to detect the local LAN IPv4 address. The function filters out localhost and link-local addresses, then returns the lowest metric interface.

The LAN IPv4 helper now falls back to parsing `ipconfig` output if PowerShell cmdlets fail. For Quest VR mode, the script will override `VITE_*` environment variables after ngrok generates its public URL, ensuring Vite receives the correct HTTPS endpoints without editing `.env`.

The Quest VR mode will set `VITE_API_BASE` and `VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL` as session environment variables, overriding `.env` for the current run. A note will remind the user that free-tier ngrok URLs change on every restart, so manual `.env` edits are needed for persistence.

Next, adding `Stop-StaleVrProxyProcesses` and related helpers to clean up stale VR proxy processes before launching.

If port 8080 is already occupied, the script will attempt to identify whether the listener is a `proxy-vr.js` Node process. It will stop and restart that process if so. Otherwise it will throw a clear error with the PID and command-line suggestion.

`Get-ListenPidsOnPort` locates processes bound to a specific port. `Stop-StaleVrProxyProcesses` stops Node processes running `proxy-vr.js` and any remaining listeners on that port. `Start-QuestVrProxyProcess` verifies `proxy-vr.js` exists, cleans up stale proxies, and throws if the port remains occupied.

`Start-QuestVrProxyProcess` now validates that `node.exe` is present on the system PATH before launching the proxy. It starts the proxy inside a new PowerShell window via `Start-Process`, passing the working directory and a startup message. A `Wait-ProxyReady` helper polls `http://127.0.0.1:8080` until the Quest VR proxy responds, timing out after 30 seconds. Next, the ngrok tunnel launcher for Quest VR is being added.

Added `Resolve-NgrokCommand` to locate `ngrok.exe` on the system PATH. `Start-QuestVrNgrokProcess` now checks for the ngrok binary before launching the tunnel. If ngrok is missing, the script prints a red error and provides instructions to download and authenticate it.

`Start-QuestVrNgrokProcess` now launches ngrok in a new PowerShell window, routing the Quest VR proxy port to the public HTTPS tunnel. A `Get-NgrokHttpsUrl` helper is being added to poll for the public HTTPS URL, with a 45-second timeout.

`Get-NgrokHttpsUrl` now queries the local ngrok API at port 4040. It extracts the public HTTPS URL from the tunnel list, falling back to the first available tunnel if none uses HTTPS. The helper returns the URL stripped of trailing slashes, or `$null` if the request times out.

The Quest VR block will be inserted between the GraphXR section and the Vite startup messages. It stores the ngrok and proxy process IDs so the cleanup block can terminate them later. A finally clause will stop any leftover ngrok or proxy processes if the script exits early. The Quest VR section begins by fetching the local LAN IP and printing a startup banner.</details></think>

`run_web_app.ps1` now supports an optional **`-QuestVR`** flag. Here’s what changed and how to use it.

## What was added

**New flag:** `-QuestVR`

| Mode | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| `.\run_web_app.ps1` | Same as before (Atlas, API, GraphXR, Vite) |
| `.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR` | All of the above **plus** VR HTTPS setup |

**With `-QuestVR`, after GraphXR is up, the script:**

1. Checks port **8080** — stops stale `proxy-vr.js` if needed, errors if port still blocked  
2. Opens a **new PowerShell window** → `node proxy-vr.js`  
3. Checks **`ngrok`** is on PATH — clear error if missing  
4. Opens a **new PowerShell window** → `ngrok http http://127.0.0.1:8080`  
5. Polls `http://127.0.0.1:4040/api/tunnels` for the **HTTPS URL**  
6. Sets **session env** for Vite (does **not** edit `.env`):
   - `VITE_API_BASE=https://<ngrok-url>`
   - `VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL=https://<ngrok-url>/viewer`
7. Prints a **Quest instructions** block with local, LAN, and HTTPS URLs

**On Ctrl+C**, it also stops the proxy/ngrok helper windows it started.

---

## How to run

```powershell
cd C:\Users\LEGION\Desktop\CSPE
.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR
```

**Prerequisites (one-time):**

- `ngrok` installed and on PATH  
- `ngrok config add-authtoken <your-token>`  
- Root `npm install` (for `http-proxy` used by `proxy-vr.js`)

---

## What you should see

1. **This terminal** — normal startup `[1]`–`[4]`, then:

```
[Quest VR] Starting HTTPS reverse proxy + ngrok...
  VR proxy ready: http://127.0.0.1:8080 (separate window)
  ngrok started (separate window). Waiting for public HTTPS URL...
  ngrok HTTPS URL: https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app
  Vite session env updated for Quest (overrides .env for this run).

========== Meta Quest 3 (WebXR) ==========
  Quest HTTPS:     https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app
  GraphXR viewer:  https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app/viewer
  ...
==========================================
```

2. **Window “CSPE Quest VR reverse proxy”** — proxy logs on `:8080`  
3. **Window “CSPE Quest VR ngrok tunnel”** — ngrok forwarding URL  
4. **Vite** — still runs in the main terminal (foreground)

---

## On Meta Quest 3

1. Open **Quest Browser**  
2. Go to the **Quest HTTPS** URL from the script (not `http://192.168.x.x`)  
3. **Transport** → **3D/VR graph** → **VR** → Enter VR  

---

## About `.env`

The script **does not auto-edit `.env`** (ngrok URLs change each run on free tier).

- **With `-QuestVR`:** Vite gets the correct HTTPS URLs for **this run** via session env (overrides `.env`).  
- **If you restart Vite alone:** copy the printed values into `.env`:

```env
VITE_API_BASE=https://<your-current-ngrok-host>
VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL=https://<your-current-ngrok-host>/viewer
```

Your `.env` still has an old ngrok URL — that’s fine for `-QuestVR` runs because the script overrides it for the session. For plain `.\run_web_app.ps1` without `-QuestVR`, remove or update those lines if they point at a dead tunnel.

Short answer: **for Quest VR, you mostly need to change how you start the app — not much in `.env`.**

## If you test on Quest with `-QuestVR`

**Run:**
```powershell
.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR
```

**You do not need to edit `.env` first.** The script sets `VITE_API_BASE` and `VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL` for that run from the **current ngrok URL**.

Use the **Quest HTTPS URL** printed in the terminal (or in the ngrok window) in the Quest browser.

---

## What to change in `.env`

These two lines are **old ngrok URLs** and will break things if you run **without** `-QuestVR` or restart Vite alone:

```env
VITE_API_BASE=https://upcountry-latter-gem.ngrok-free.dev
VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL=https://upcountry-latter-gem.ngrok-free.dev/viewer
```

**Pick one:**

| How you work | What to do |
|--------------|------------|
| **Always use `-QuestVR` for Quest** | **Delete** those two lines (or comment them out). The script sets them each run. |
| **Sometimes restart Vite without the script** | After `.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR`, copy the **new** URLs from the terminal into `.env`. Update them **every time ngrok gives a new URL**. |

**Leave everything else in `.env` as is** (Mapbox, IDFM, Azure, Atlas planner settings).

1. **ngrok** installed + authenticated: `ngrok config add-authtoken <token>`
2. **Root deps** for the proxy: `npm install` in `C:\Users\LEGION\Desktop\CSPE` (for `http-proxy`)

```powershell
.\run_web_app.ps1
```

Remove or ignore the ngrok lines in `.env` so Vite uses the normal local proxy (`http://127.0.0.1:8787` via `/api`).

**Bottom line:** delete the stale ngrok lines from `.env`, use `.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR` for Quest, and only paste ngrok URLs into `.env` if you need them when Vite isn’t started by that script.

_**User**_

.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR once i ran this i can access on both my computer and meta quest?


---

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Yes — **one run** starts everything for **both**, but you use **different URLs** on each device.

## On your PC

You can open:

| URL | Works for |
|-----|-----------|
| `http://127.0.0.1:5173` | Normal use (map, chat, 3D tab) |
| `http://<your-LAN-IP>:5173` | Same, from another device on Wi‑Fi (optional) |
| `https://<ngrok-url>` | Same app through the tunnel (same as Quest) |

PC does **not** need HTTPS for normal browsing.

---

## On Meta Quest 3

Use **only the ngrok HTTPS URL** from the terminal or ngrok window, for example:

```text
https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app
```

- Open it in the **Quest browser**
- **WebXR / VR requires HTTPS** — `http://192.168.x.x:5173` on Quest will **not** enter VR
- Transport → **3D/VR graph** → **VR** → Enter VR in the headset

---

## What `-QuestVR` starts

| Service | Port | Who uses it |
|---------|------|-------------|
| Vite (main UI) | 5173 | PC directly |
| GraphXR | 3000 | Via proxy / ngrok |
| Product API | 8787 | Via proxy / ngrok |
| **proxy-vr.js** | 8080 | Bundles all three for ngrok |
| **ngrok** | → 8080 | Quest (and optionally PC) |

So: **same stack, one launch** — PC via localhost (easiest), Quest via the **https://…ngrok…** link.

---

## Quick checklist

1. Run `.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR`
2. Wait for the **Quest HTTPS** line in the main terminal
3. **PC:** `http://127.0.0.1:5173`
4. **Quest:** paste the **https://** ngrok URL in the browser

If the ngrok URL changes next time you run the script, use the **new** URL on Quest (free ngrok URLs often change each session).

_**User**_

how do i know the ngrok link

---

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

You’ll get the ngrok link in **three places** when you run:

```powershell
.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR
```

## 1. Main terminal (easiest)

After startup, look for a block like:

```text
[Quest VR] ...
  ngrok HTTPS URL: https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app

========== Meta Quest 3 (WebXR) ==========
  Quest HTTPS:     https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app
  GraphXR viewer:  https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app/viewer
```

**Use the `Quest HTTPS` line on your Meta Quest.**

---

## 2. Ngrok window

A **second PowerShell window** opens with ngrok. Look for a line like:

```text
Forwarding   https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app -> http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

Copy the **`https://...`** part (not the `http://127.0.0.1:8080` part).

---

## 3. Ngrok web UI (on your PC)

With ngrok running, open in a **PC browser**:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:4040
```

You’ll see the public URL under the tunnel details.

---

## If you don’t see a URL

- Wait a few seconds after the ngrok window opens.
- Check the ngrok window for errors (often **authtoken** not set):

```powershell
ngrok config add-authtoken YOUR_TOKEN
```

- Make sure ngrok is installed and on PATH: `ngrok version`

---

**On Quest:** paste only the **`https://...`** link into the Meta Quest browser — not `127.0.0.1` or `192.168.x.x`.

Your log shows **why Quest VR failed** — and it’s fixable.

## What went wrong

Two things:

1. **Missing dependency** — `http-proxy` wasn’t installed at the repo root, so `proxy-vr.js` likely crashed in its window.
2. **Bad health check** — the script tested `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` **before Vite started**. The proxy forwards `/` to port 5173, which wasn’t up yet → timeout.

Because of that, **ngrok never started**, so no HTTPS URL was printed.

---

## What we fixed

- Added `/health` on the proxy (doesn’t need Vite).
- Script now waits for port 8080 + `/health` instead of `/`.
- Script runs `npm install` at repo root if `http-proxy` is missing.

---

## What you should do now

1. **Stop the current run** — `Ctrl+C` in the terminal running the app.

2. **Install proxy deps once** (if you haven’t):
   ```powershell
   cd C:\Users\LEGION\Desktop\CSPE
   npm install
   ```

3. **Start again:**
   ```powershell
   .\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR
   ```

4. **Look for these lines** (success):
   ```text
   VR proxy ready: http://127.0.0.1:8080 (separate window)
   ngrok started (separate window). Waiting for public HTTPS URL...
   ngrok HTTPS URL: https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app

   Quest HTTPS:     https://xxxx.ngrok-free.app
   ```

5. **Two extra windows** should open:
   - **CSPE Quest VR reverse proxy** — should say `VR proxy running on http://0.0.0.0:8080`
   - **CSPE Quest VR ngrok tunnel** — shows `Forwarding https://... -> http://127.0.0.1:8080`

6. **Quest browser:** open the **`https://...`** URL (from the main terminal or ngrok window).

---

## Right now (your current run)

- **PC:** `http://127.0.0.1:5173` works.
- **Quest VR:** won’t work until you restart with the fix — no ngrok URL was created this time.

If it fails again, check the **proxy PowerShell window** for a red error and paste it here.
