ViewerClient.tsx already handles embedded mode correctly by hiding headers and adjusting overlays. ShellCommandListener.tsx will revert its graph3d commands to setTransportViz("graph3d") instead of opening a new tab. The standalone openGraph3dViewerInNewTab helper in graph3dSync.ts can be removed since the viewer will stay on the same page.

The old fingerprint sync timer will be restored for graph3d view. Live sync will remain enabled while the viewer is active. Exiting graph3d will happen by switching the visualization mode back to geographic or 3D map.

The fullscreen graph3d mode will ignore the existing mapChromeHidden state and always hide all chrome via the dedicated CSS class. The map iframe will be hidden while the graph3d viewer is active. Need to verify error and loading states for the graph3d view.</details></think>

```
import { ToolRail } from "./ToolRail";
import { AtlasRailPanel } from "./AtlasRailPanel";
import { AgentContextSync } from "./AgentContextSync";
import { ShellCommandListener } from "./ShellCommandListener";
import { MapFocusHotkey } from "./MapFocusHotkey";
import { TransportMode } from "../modes/TransportMode";
import { VisualBoardMode } from "../modes/VisualBoardMode";
import { MemoryMode } from "../modes/MemoryMode";
import { MusicMode } from "../modes/MusicMode";
import { useAppStore } from "../store";

export function AppShell() {
  const mode = useAppStore((s) =&gt; s.mode);
  const setMode = useAppStore((s) =&gt; s.setMode);
  const mapChromeHidden = useAppStore((s) =&gt; s.transportMapChromeHidden);
  const mapFocusActive = mode === "transport" &amp;&amp; mapChromeHidden;

  return (
    &lt;div className={&#96;app-root${mapFocusActive ? " app-root--map-focus" : ""}&#96;}&gt;
      &lt;ShellCommandListener /&gt;
      &lt;AgentContextSync /&gt;
      &lt;MapFocusHotkey /&gt;
      &lt;div className="app-root__body"&gt;
        &lt;ToolRail mode={mode} onMode={setMode} /&gt;
        &lt;div className="app-shell__main"&gt;
        {/* Keep Transport mounted for the session so the map iframe does not reload when switching modes */}
        &lt;div
          style={{
            flex: 1,
            minHeight: 0,
            display: mode === "transport" ? "flex" : "none",
            flexDirection: "column",
            overflow: "hidden",
          }}
          aria-hidden={mode !== "transport"}
        &gt;
          &lt;TransportMode /&gt;
        &lt;/div&gt;
        {mode === "visual" &amp;&amp; (
          &lt;div style={{ flex: 1, minHeight: 0, display: "flex", flexDirection: "column", overflow: "hidden" }}&gt;
            &lt;VisualBoardMode /&gt;
          &lt;/div&gt;
        )}
        {mode === "memory" &amp;&amp; (
          &lt;div style={{ flex: 1, minHeight: 0, display: "flex", flexDirection: "column", overflow: "hidden" }}&gt;
            &lt;MemoryMode /&gt;
          &lt;/div&gt;
        )}
        {mode === "music" &amp;&amp; (
          &lt;div style={{ flex: 1, minHeight: 0, display: "flex", flexDirection: "column", overflow: "hidden" }}&gt;
            &lt;MusicMode /&gt;
          &lt;/div&gt;
        )}
        {!mapFocusActive &amp;&amp; &lt;AtlasRailPanel /&gt;}
        &lt;/div&gt;
      &lt;/div&gt;
    &lt;/div&gt;
  );
}
```

3D/VR is back on the same page, fullscreen, with Atlas and transport chrome hidden.

### Behavior
| Action | Result |
|--------|--------|
| **3D/VR graph** button (or Atlas `graph3d` command) | GraphXR loads inline in the map area, full viewport |
| **Atlas rail / panels / map controls** | Hidden while in graph3d mode |
| **← Map** (top-left) | Returns to geographic map |
| Route / selection changes | Live sync still pushes updates to the embedded viewer |

### What changed
- **`TransportMode.tsx`** — Restored embedded iframe (`graph3dViewerUrl`), removed the new-tab popup and the effect that forced geographic mode. Fullscreen class hides all transport HUD; only a minimal **← Map** exit button remains.
- **`AppShell.tsx`** — Hides `AtlasRailPanel` when `transportViz === "graph3d"`.
- **`ShellCommandListener.tsx`** — Atlas commands set `transportViz("graph3d")` instead of opening a popup.
- **`transport.css` / `modeShell.css`** — Fullscreen styles for graph3d mode.

The GraphXR viewer still uses `embedded=1`, so its own standalone header/back link stays hidden; in-viewer VR controls (Reset, Labels, VR, etc.) remain available inside the iframe.

_**User**_

Create a Markdown file that contains two clear project architecture diagrams for the CSPE project.

Do not modify the application code. Only create a new Markdown documentation file.

Goal:
I need these diagrams to reuse them in a PowerPoint presentation. They must be readable, not overloaded, and understandable by someone who does not know the codebase.

Before creating the diagrams, inspect the full project structure and use the real architecture from the codebase. Do not invent components. Decide yourself what technical elements are important enough to show.

Create the file here:

docs/presentation_architecture_diagrams.md

The file must contain:

1. A first diagram: “Global project architecture”

This diagram should show the project as three big functional blocks:

- AI Agent / Atlas
- Transport backend / graph processing
- Visualization layer

The goal is to show how the whole system is organized globally.

Keep it high-level and presentation-friendly. Inside each block, include only the important sub-elements you find in the project, such as APIs, services, models, data sources, tools, frontend parts, visualization modules, etc., but avoid too much code-level detail.

The diagram should make clear:
- how the user interacts with the system
- how Atlas and/or the manual UI enter the system
- where the transport data and graph logic are handled
- how results are sent to visualizations
- what the final outputs are, such as routes, POIs, map views, 3D/VR graph, etc.

2. A second diagram: “Example request flow”

This diagram should show one concrete flow from user request to visual output.

Use a realistic example from the project, such as:
“Find a route from Nation to Aéroport d’Orly”
or another route/POI example if it better matches the current code.

The goal is to show the sequence:
user request → Atlas/manual UI → backend/API → transport graph logic → result → map/3D/VR visualization.

This diagram should be more step-by-step than the first one.

3. Add short explanations under each diagram

For each diagram, add:
- a short paragraph explaining what the diagram shows
- a short list of the main components involved
- a short note about why this architecture is useful for the project

Diagram format:
Use Mermaid diagrams inside Markdown code blocks.
Prefer flowchart diagrams.
Make the diagrams visually clean and not too dense.
Use grouped subgraphs when useful.
Use clear labels in English or simple French, but keep the wording presentation-friendly.

Important constraints:
- Do not create a huge unreadable diagram.
- Do not go too deep into implementation details.
- Do not include every file or every function.
- Do not modify source code.
- Do not modify the PowerPoint.
- Do not modify existing documentation unless necessary.
- Only create the Markdown file with the two diagrams and explanations.

After creating the file, summarize:
- where the file was created
- what the two diagrams represent
- any assumptions you made

2. **Example request flow** — Step-by-step flow for *“Find a route from Nation to Aéroport d’Orly”*: user → Atlas or manual UI → planner/tools → Product Shell API → GTFS graph routing → shell commands → React → map (and optional GraphXR).

- **Shell command queue** is shown as the bridge from Atlas tools to the React UI, since Atlas does not render maps directly.
- **IDFM API** is included as an optional enrichment source, not the primary routing graph (routing uses the local GTFS bundle).
- **Quest VR / ngrok** is omitted to keep slides readable; the doc mentions default dev ports only in a short PowerPoint note at the bottom.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The default GTFS source is `data/gtfs/`. The script `scripts/rebuild_routing_bundle.py` reads `stops.txt` to define the graph nodes.

Ride edges require `routes.txt`, `trips.txt`, and `stop_times.txt`. `transfers.txt` is optional. `calendar.txt`, `calendar_dates.txt`, `shapes.txt`, `frequencies.txt`, `agency.txt`, and `feed_info.txt` are not used.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

The routing graph is built from **`data/gtfs/`** (default in `scripts/rebuild_routing_bundle.py`) via `load_gtfs()` in `src/core/graph_loader.py`. Only **5 GTFS files** are read; nothing else from the GTFS zip is used for nodes/edges.

## GTFS files used

| GTFS file | Required? | Role in the graph |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| **`stops.txt`** | Yes | **Nodes**: each `stop_id` is a graph node. Uses `stop_id`, `stop_name`, `stop_lat`, `stop_lon`. |
| **`stop_times.txt`** | Yes | **Ride edges**: consecutive stops on the same trip (`trip_id`, `stop_id`, `stop_sequence`). |
| **`trips.txt`** | Yes | Links each trip to a route (`trip_id`, `route_id`). |
| **`routes.txt`** | Yes | Mode/line on ride edges (`route_id`, `route_type`, `route_short_name`, `route_long_name`). |
| **`transfers.txt`** | Optional | **GTFS transfer edges** (`from_stop_id`, `to_stop_id`, `transfer_type`, `min_transfer_time`). Skipped if the file is missing. |

## GTFS files **not** used for nodes/edges

These are **not** read by `load_gtfs()` or the bundle builder:

- `calendar.txt`, `calendar_dates.txt` — no service-day filtering in graph build  
- `shapes.txt` — distances come from haversine between stop coordinates, not shapes  
- `frequencies.txt`, `agency.txt`, `feed_info.txt`, `stop_times` extras, etc.

So the graph is a **topology graph** (who connects to whom), not a timetable-accurate schedule graph.

---

## How nodes are created

1. **`stops.txt`** → `build_pos_all()` → coordinates for every stop.  
2. **Edges** are built from the files above.  
3. **`build_graph()`** adds a node for each endpoint of an edge, then attaches `stop_name`, `lat`, `lon` from `stops.txt`.

A stop with no ride or transfer edge does **not** appear as a node in the routing graph.

---

## How edges are created (3 types)

### 1. Ride edges (`edge_kind = "ride"`)

From: **`stop_times.txt` + `trips.txt` + `routes.txt`**, with distances from **`stops.txt`** coords.

Logic in `build_ride_edges()`:

- Sort `stop_times` by `trip_id` + `stop_sequence`
- Link each stop to the **next stop on the same trip**
- Join `trips` → `routes` for mode (`route_type` → metro/rail/tram/bus/other) and line labels
- Merge duplicate stop pairs; set `distance_m`, `time_s`, `cost`, `weight_m`

### 2. GTFS transfer edges (`edge_kind = "transfer"`)

From: **`transfers.txt`** (+ **`stops.txt`** for walking distance).

- Skips `transfer_type == 3` (forbidden)
- Only between stops that already appear on ride edges
- Does not duplicate pairs already connected by a ride edge
- Time from `min_transfer_time`, or estimated walk time from coordinates

### 3. Inferred transfer edges (`edge_kind = "transfer"`)

From: **`stops.txt` only** (not a separate GTFS file).

- Same normalized stop name within **400 m**
- Any two stops within **200 m**
- **180 s** transfer penalty
- Fills gaps where `transfers.txt` is incomplete

All three are merged in `combine_edges()` and saved to **`data/derived/routing/graph_bundle.pkl`**.

---

## Build command

```bash
python scripts/rebuild_routing_bundle.py --gtfs-dir data/gtfs
```

Pipeline (from `rebuild_routing_bundle.py`):

```
load_gtfs()
  → build_ride_edges()
  → build_gtfs_transfer_edges()
  → build_transfer_edges()   # inferred
  → combine_edges()
  → graph_bundle.pkl
```

---

## Related but **not** graph nodes/edges

- **`parent_station`** — used later in `station_layer.py` for **station grouping in the UI**, from normalized parquet (`data/normalized/...`), not when building the pickle edges.
- **`stop_popup_index.parquet`** — enriches node display (lines, modes) when the bundle is loaded in `cache_bundle.py`, built from the same GTFS chain (`stop_times` + `trips` + `routes`), not a separate GTFS file.

---

**Bottom line:** graph **nodes** = `stop_id` from **`stops.txt`** (those that appear on edges). Graph **edges** = consecutive **`stop_times`** (via **`trips`** + **`routes`**) plus **`transfers.txt`** plus **inferred transfers from `stops.txt` geometry/names**.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

There are two layers: **how a path is chosen**, and **how edge costs are computed** (mostly for reporting, not for choosing the path today).

## 1. Main path-finding principle (what actually picks the route)

The core algorithm is **shortest path on an unweighted graph** = **fewest edges (fewest “hops”)**.

In code (`src/core/queries.py`):

```python
path = nx.shortest_path(G, a, b)  # no weight= argument
```

That is NetworkX’s default **unweighted** shortest path (BFS-style on an undirected graph). So the objective is effectively:

\[
\min \; |\text{path}| - 1 \quad \text{(number of edges)}
\]

**Not** “shortest time” or “shortest distance” — even though each edge stores `time_s`, `cost`, and `distance_m`. The `strategy` and `use_weights` parameters exist but are **ignored**; routing is forced to `"hops"`.

For **station-to-station** routing, CSPE tries every platform pair between the two stations and keeps the best path using this tie-break (`station_layer.py`):

1. Fewest hops  
2. Then smallest total `distance_m`  
3. Then smallest total `time_s`

---

## 2. Equations used when **building** the graph (edge weights)

These formulas define what each edge “costs” in data, but **today they do not drive path selection**.

### Distance between two stops (Haversine)

Used for ride edges and transfers (`graph_loader.py`):

\[
d = 2R \arcsin\left(\sqrt{\sin^2\frac{\Delta\phi}{2} + \cos\phi_1\cos\phi_2\sin^2\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}}\right)
\]

with \(R = 6\,371\,000\) m.

### Ride time on an edge

\[
t_{\text{ride}} = \frac{d}{\ v_{\text{mode}}}
\]

Mode speeds (m/s): metro 12, rail 16, tram 8, bus 5, other 6. If several modes share an edge, the **fastest** mode speed is used.

Also: `cost = time_s`, `weight_m = distance_m` on ride edges.

### Transfer time

- **GTFS transfer:** use `min_transfer_time` from `transfers.txt` if &gt; 0, else walk time \(d / 1.4\) m/s.  
- **Inferred transfer:** walk time plus **180 s penalty**:

\[
\text{cost}_{\text{transfer}} = \frac{d}{1.4} + 180
\]

---

## 3. Equations used **after** the path is found (summary only)

Once the hop-minimal path is chosen, `summarize_path()` totals metrics along that path:

\[
D = \sum_{(u,v) \in \text{path}} \text{distance\_m}(u,v)
\]

\[
T = \sum_{(u,v) \in \text{path}} \text{time\_s}(u,v)
\]

\[
\text{transfers} = \#\{(u,v) : \text{edge\_kind}(u,v) = \text{"transfer"}\}
\]

Those values are what the UI shows (distance, time, number of transfers) — but they **did not** determine which path was picked.

---

## One-sentence summary for a presentation

> **We model Île-de-France transport as a graph (stops = nodes, ride/transfer links = edges), then compute a route with classical graph shortest-path — today minimizing the number of edges, not total travel time — and we report distance, estimated time, and transfers by summing edge attributes along that path.**

---

## If you want “the real” routing equation (not implemented yet)

The natural next step would be **Dijkstra** with edge weight = `cost` (time):

\[
\min \sum_{(u,v) \in \text{path}} \text{cost}(u,v)
\]

The data is already on the edges; the code would need to call something like `nx.shortest_path(G, a, b, weight="cost")` instead of unweighted `shortest_path`. That would align path **choice** with the time formulas above.

Slide 6 — Backend et API 

Le backend est un serveur FastAPI. Il joue le rôle de point central entre l’interface, l’agent IA, les données transport et les visualisations. 

 

Quand le frontend a besoin d’une route, il n’accède pas directement aux fichiers GTFS ou au graphe. Il envoie une requête API au backend. Par exemple, une requête POST peut contenir la station de départ, la station d’arrivée, le mode de transport et les options de visualisation. 

 

Le backend reçoit cette requête, appelle le moteur transport, récupère le résultat du calcul, puis renvoie une réponse structurée. 

 

Cette réponse peut être du JSON, par exemple pour une route ou une liste de stations. Elle peut aussi être du HTML généré pour une carte Mapbox affichée dans l’interface. 

 

L’intérêt d’utiliser une API est de garder une architecture propre. Le frontend demande une action, le backend traite, puis le frontend affiche. Ça permet aussi à Atlas d’utiliser les mêmes fonctionnalités, parce que lui aussi peut déclencher des appels vers le backend.

Your slide explanation is **mostly correct**. A few small refinements for the defense:

- **Route vs map** are separate API calls: `POST /api/transport/route` sends stop/station IDs + graph mode (`metro`, `use_lcc`, etc.), not map viz options. Map options go to `POST /api/transport/map`.
- The frontend never reads GTFS; the server uses a **pre-built** `graph_bundle.pkl`, not raw GTFS on every request.
- Atlas uses the **same transport APIs**, and sometimes also **`/api/shell/enqueue`** to sync the UI.

I created **`docs/backend_api_slide_diagram.md`** with:

Created **`docs/atlas_agent_slide_diagram.md`** — a companion to your backend slide, focused entirely on Atlas.

### What's inside (6 diagrams)

1. **Global architecture** — User → React rail → Product Shell → Atlas (:5055) → planner/tools → same `:8787` APIs + shell queue → map updates  
2. **Text chat full turn** — `POST /api/chat` → `/text` → planner → tools → poll `/ui` → chat bubbles + shell commands → map  
3. **Voice hold-to-talk** — `input-mode: voice` → Realtime → poll `/api/atlas/ui` every ~480 ms  
4. **Planner pipeline** — shortcuts → intent router → domain routers → tool plan → `tool_executor`  
5. **How Atlas updates the map** — tools → `shell/enqueue` → SSE/poll → Zustand → TransportMode (Atlas never touches the DOM)  
6. **Concrete example** — “Nation → Orly” with `cspe_search_stops` + `cspe_compute_route`

Also included: tool table, text vs voice vs manual UI comparison, oral script in French, common mistakes, and PowerPoint export tips.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
There are two main JSON output formats for the planner. One is per-step: it returns status, tool, arguments, and a final summary. The other is multi-step: it returns status, a steps array, a clarifying question, and a final summary. The exact structure depends on which specification version you are following.

The planner prompt combines system instructions, a tool catalog, context, and the user message. It calls the OpenAI Chat Completions API with response_format set to json_object. The returned JSON is parsed and normalized into fields like tool_name and args. Shortcuts are tried first to avoid unnecessary LLM calls.</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Your mental model is **almost exactly right**. Here is how it works in CSPE, in simple terms.

## Short answer

Yes: you send the user’s text to a model **with instructions + a list of allowed tools**, and the model returns **JSON** (not free chat for that step). Your Python code **parses, validates, and executes** that JSON by calling real functions (`cspe_compute_route`, etc.). The friendly sentence the user sees in chat is often a **second** model step **after** tools run.

OpenAI is used as a **tool picker**, not as the routing engine.

---

## The full flow (text mode)

```
User: "Route from Nation to Orly"
        ↓
1. Shortcuts first (no AI) — regex like "open 3D map"
        ↓ if no match
2. OpenAI planner (or Ollama if configured)
        ↓
3. JSON: { status, tool, arguments, ... }
        ↓
4. validate_planner_decision() — tool exists? args OK?
        ↓
5. execute_tool("cspe_compute_route", args) → HTTP to :8787
        ↓
6. Maybe loop (another tool if status = "continue")
        ↓
7. OpenAI writes final reply text for the user
```

---

## What you actually send to OpenAI (planner)

It is **not** just the raw user sentence alone. The planner builds a **user message** that includes:

- **ALLOWED TOOLS** — compact catalog from `tools_registry.json` (name, description, required args)
- **ROUTER CONTEXT** — last tool, last topic, follow-up hints
- **WORLD_STATE** — transport context from `/api/agent/context`
- **RECENT_EVENTS** — short history
- **STEP_RESULTS** — results of tools already run this turn
- **USER** — the actual user text

Plus a **system prompt** (`_PLANNER_SYSTEM` in `agent_planner.py`) that says roughly:

> “You are a planner. Reply **only** with JSON. Pick one tool and its arguments, or say you’re done / need clarification.”

The API call uses **Chat Completions** with:

- `response_format: { "type": "json_object" }` → forces JSON output  
- `temperature: 0` → more deterministic  
- model like `gpt-4o` (or `ATLAS_OPENAI_PLANNER_MODEL`)

So: **structured prompt in → JSON out**, not “chat freely about transport.”

---

## What JSON looks like (one planning step)

Simplified shape (from `LOCAL_PLANNER.md` / planner code):

```json
{
  "status": "continue",
  "tool": "cspe_compute_route",
  "arguments": {
    "from_query": "Nation",
    "to_query": "Aéroport d'Orly",
    "mode": "all"
  },
  "final_summary": ""
}
```

**`status` meanings:**

| status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `continue` | Run **one** tool, then maybe plan again |
| `done` | Finished after tool(s) |
| `clarify` | Ask user something (`final_summary` = question) |
| `direct` | Answer without tools (pure Q&A) |

If invalid JSON or unknown tool → validation fails → retry/repair or fallback (Ollama/OpenAI again).

---

## What your code does with that JSON

1. **`json.loads()`** the model output  
2. **`validate_planner_decision()`** — tool name must be in allowed set (e.g. only transport tools for route questions)  
3. **`execute_tool(name, args)`** — normal Python; e.g. `cspe_compute_route` does:
   - `GET /api/transport/stops/search` for “Nation” and “Orly”
   - `POST /api/transport/route`
   - `POST /api/shell/enqueue` so the map updates  
4. If **`status == "continue"`**, loop (up to ~8 steps): e.g. search stops → compute route → open graph3d  
5. After tools, another OpenAI call often generates the **natural language answer** the user reads in the rail

So: **model chooses the tool + args; your code runs the tool.**

---

## OpenAI is used for **three different jobs**

| Job | When | What it does |
|-----|------|----------------|
| **Planner** | User sends text | JSON: which `cspe_*` tool + arguments |
| **Final reply** | After tools run | Normal text: “Voici l’itinéraire…” |
| **Realtime voice** | Hold-to-talk | Speech in/out; planner/tools can still run in the background |

The **graph shortest path** is **never** computed by the LLM — that is NetworkX in Python on the server.

---

## When OpenAI is **not** used

**Deterministic shortcuts** (`planner_shortcuts.py`) handle things like:

- “Open transport map”
- “Show 3D graph”
- Simple patterns

Those return the same kind of tool decision **without** calling the model (&lt; 200 ms).

There is also an **intent router** (central + domain routers) that can classify “this is a route / POI / 3D request” before or alongside the planner — tests in `tests/test_intent_routing.py` show that path.

---

## Optional: local Ollama instead of OpenAI for planning

With `ATLAS_PLANNER_BACKEND=local` or `auto`, **Ollama** (e.g. `qwen2.5:3b-instruct`) does the **same job** — JSON tool + args. OpenAI may still write the **final spoken/text reply**. Same pipeline, different model for step 2 in the diagram above.

---

## Analogy for your presentation

Think of OpenAI as a **dispatcher**:

- You give it: user request + menu of actions (`cspe_compute_route`, `cspe_explore_area`, …)
- It returns: **work order JSON** (“call this function with these parameters”)
- Your backend **executes** the work order on real APIs and the graph
- Then the model **summarizes** the result for the user

You did **not** train it on GTFS. You **configured** it with prompts, JSON schema, and a tool registry.

---

## One line for the jury

> « On envoie le texte utilisateur à OpenAI avec la liste des outils autorisés ; le modèle répond en JSON (`tool` + `arguments`) ; notre code valide ce JSON et exécute l’outil correspondant sur le backend FastAPI ; la réponse naturelle vient ensuite, mais le calcul d’itinéraire reste dans NetworkX, pas dans le LLM. »

If you want, I can add this as a short section in `docs/atlas_agent_slide_diagram.md`.

---

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Planner behavior is defined in **several places**, not one single string. Here is where each layer lives and what it does.

---

## 1. Main OpenAI planner instructions (tool picking)

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/agent_planner.py`

The **system prompt** is the constant `_PLANNER_SYSTEM` (rules, JSON schema, which tools to use):

```107:137:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/agent_planner.py
_PLANNER_SYSTEM = """You are Atlas Planner for CSPE (transport, POI, map, 3D graph).

Output ONE JSON object only (no markdown). Use strict tool names from ALLOWED TOOLS.

SCHEMA:
{
  "status": "continue" | "done" | "clarify" | "direct",
  "steps": [{"tool": "tool_name", "arguments": {}, "reason": "optional"}],
  ...
}

RULES:
- Natural-language commands: choose the minimal valid tool chain in "steps" (ordered).
- Routes: use cspe_compute_route with from_query, to_query, sync_ui:true (not cspe_route).
- Stop lookup: cspe_search_stops with query ...
...
"""
```

It is sent to OpenAI in **`_plan_next_step_openai()`** together with a **user message** that includes the tool list, context, and the user text:

```231:271:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/agent_planner.py
def _plan_next_step_openai(
    *,
    user_text: str,
    tools_catalog_text: str,
    ...
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    msg = (
        "ALLOWED TOOLS:\n"
        f"{tools_catalog_text}\n\n"
        "ROUTER CONTEXT:\n"
        f"{context_text.strip() or '(none)'}\n\n"
        "WORLD_STATE:\n"
        ...
        "USER:\n"
        f"{user_text}\n\n"
        "Return planner JSON with steps[] when multiple actions are needed."
    )
    resp = _CLIENT.chat.completions.create(
        model=PLANNER_MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": _PLANNER_SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user", "content": msg},
        ],
        temperature=0,
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        max_tokens=800,
    )
```

**Entry point:** `run_planner_turn()` in the same file calls this via `resolve_planner_plan()` → `openai_plan_fn` (around lines 385–404).

---

## 2. Tool list sent to the model (not behavior rules)

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/tools_registry.json`  
Descriptions and argument schemas for each tool (`cspe_compute_route`, etc.).

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/tool_instructions.py`  
Builds the compact text block injected as `ALLOWED TOOLS:`:

```18:41:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/tool_instructions.py
def build_router_catalog() -> str:
    """
    Compact tool catalog for the semantic router prompt.
    ...
    """
    tool_names = list_tools()
    lines: list[str] = ["TOOLS (router view):"]
    for name in tool_names:
        tool_info: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = get_tool_info(name) or {}
        desc = (tool_info.get("description") or "").strip()
        ...
        lines.append(f"- {name}: {desc} ({req}, {opt})")
    return "\n".join(lines)
```

So: **`_PLANNER_SYSTEM` = how to behave**; **`tools_registry.json` + `build_router_catalog()` = what tools exist**.

---

## 3. Routing before OpenAI (shortcuts, no LLM)

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/planner_pipeline.py`  
Order: shortcuts → OpenAI → Ollama fallback.

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/planner_shortcuts.py`  
Regex/rules (e.g. “open 3D graph”) — **no OpenAI call**.

---

## 4. Intent router path (when enabled)

If `intent_router` is on, **`run_planner_turn()`** uses `resolve_intent_plan()` instead of going straight to `_plan_next_step_openai` (see `agent_planner.py` lines 370–383).

Intent extraction has its **own** system prompt:

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/intent_extractor.py`

```16:55:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/intent_extractor.py
_INTENT_SYSTEM = """You are Atlas Intent Extractor for CSPE (Paris transport, POI, map, 3D graph).

Output ONE JSON object only. Do NOT output tool names (no cspe_* as execution).
...
- Route A to B → domain transport, intent route; ui_action true if user wants map route shown.
...
"""
```

That JSON is mapped to tools by **domain routers** (Python), not by the model choosing `cspe_*` directly.

---

## 5. Local Ollama planner (alternative to OpenAI for tools)

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/local_planner.py`

```49:65:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/router/local_planner.py
_LOCAL_SYSTEM = """Atlas Local Planner. Output ONE JSON object only.
...
- Prefer cspe_compute_route for A→B routes; cspe_search_stops for stop lookup.
...
"""

_REPAIR_SYSTEM = """Fix JSON. Keys only: status, tool, arguments, final_summary."""
```

Same idea as OpenAI: system instructions + user payload → JSON → `validate_planner_decision()`.

---

## 6. Final user-facing reply (voice) — different instructions

This is **not** the planner. The Realtime model is told **not** to pick tools:

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/orchestrator.py`

```137:167:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/orchestrator.py
        base_instructions = (
            "You are Atlas.\n"
            ...
            "ROLE:\n"
            "- You are the answer generator.\n"
            "- Tool routing/execution is handled by the system (you do not call tools).\n\n"
            ...
            "WHEN YOU SEE A DATA BLOCK:\n"
            "- If you receive AGENT_PLAN_RESULTS: summarize the outcome for the user using only those facts.\n"
            ...
        )
```

After tools run, `agent_planner.py` builds an **`AGENT_PLAN_RESULTS`** block (`_build_injection_block`, ~lines 274–299) and sends it to the Realtime model so it can phrase the answer.

---

## Quick map

| What | Where | OpenAI call? |
|------|--------|--------------|
| Planner behavior + JSON schema | `agent_planner.py` → `_PLANNER_SYSTEM` | Yes (`_plan_next_step_openai`) |
| Tool definitions | `tools_registry.json` + `tool_instructions.py` | In user message |
| Shortcuts | `planner_shortcuts.py` | No |
| Intent understanding | `intent_extractor.py` → `_INTENT_SYSTEM` | Yes (if intent router on) |
| Local planner | `local_planner.py` → `_LOCAL_SYSTEM` | Ollama, not OpenAI |
| Spoken/text answer style | `orchestrator.py` → `base_instructions` | Realtime session |

---

## Model name

**File:** `src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/planner_config.py`  
Default: `gpt-4o` via `ATLAS_PLANNER_MODEL` / `ATLAS_ROUTER_MODEL`.

---

**Bottom line:** the main “behave like this and return JSON” instructions for the OpenAI planner are **`_PLANNER_SYSTEM`** in `agent_planner.py`, sent as the **`system`** message in **`_plan_next_step_openai()`** (~lines 257–266). The user message adds tools, context, world state, and the actual user text.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Here is a **simple soutenance script** you can put on the slide or read aloud. It matches your diagram and the real Atlas flow.

---

## What to say in one sentence

> « Quand l’utilisateur parle ou écrit à Atlas, on ne laisse pas le modèle faire n’importe quoi : on passe d’abord par des **raccourcis rapides**, puis si besoin par un **planificateur IA** qui choisit un **outil** ; ensuite c’est **notre code Python** qui exécute l’outil sur le backend et met à jour la carte. »

---

## The funnel (top → bottom)

### 1. User message
« L’entrée, c’est le message utilisateur — texte dans le chat ou transcription vocale. »

### 2. Fast paths first (no heavy AI)
« Avant d’appeler OpenAI, on teste des **chemins déterministes** : »

- **`try_ui_settings_intent`** — petites actions UI claires (changer la viz, ouvrir la 3D, etc.)
- **`try_deterministic_intent`** — motifs / mots-clés connus (regex, raccourcis)

« Si on reconnaît la demande, on va **directement** à l’exécution d’un outil. C’est rapide et fiable. »

### 3. If it’s not obvious → understand the intent
« Sinon, on structure la demande : **domaine** (transport, POI, carte, 3D), **intention** (route, explorer, info gare…), **entités** (Nation, Orly, restaurant…). »

That’s **`StructuredIntent`** in the diagram.

### 4. Route to the right “specialist”
« Un **routeur central** envoie la demande au bon module : »

| Module | Examples |
|--------|----------|
| **transport** | route, exploration, graph3d |
| **poi** | POIs nearby |
| **visual_3d / map_ui** | carte, couche graphique, 3D |

« Chaque domaine sait quels **outils CSPE** (`cspe_*`) sont autorisés. »

### 5. Build a plan (OpenAI / Ollama if needed)
« Si les raccourcis ne suffisent pas, le **planificateur** (OpenAI par défaut, ou Ollama en local) reçoit : »

- les **instructions** (`_PLANNER_SYSTEM` in `agent_planner.py`)
- la **liste des outils** (`tools_registry.json`)
- le **contexte** (dernière gare, dernière exploration…)
- le **message utilisateur**

« Il répond en **JSON** : quel outil appeler, avec quels arguments — pas en texte libre pour agir sur l’app. »

### 6. Execute (`tool_executor`)
« Notre code **valide** le JSON (outil connu ? arguments OK ?), puis **exécute** l’outil : »

- appels HTTP vers le **Product Shell** (`:8787`) — route, exploration, recherche…
- **`shell enqueue`** — commandes pour que React mette à jour la carte

« **OpenAI ne calcule pas l’itinéraire** : il choisit *compute route* ; **NetworkX** sur le serveur calcule le chemin. »

### 7. Reply to the user
« Ensuite Atlas produit la **réponse en langage naturel** (texte ou voix), à partir des **résultats réels** des outils — pas en inventant un trajet. »

---

## Short version for the slide (bullet points)

**Title suggestion:** *Atlas — decision making*

- User message (text / voice)
- **Fast path:** UI shortcuts & keyword rules → tool if match
- **Otherwise:** intent → domain router (transport / POI / map / 3D)
- **Planner (OpenAI / Ollama):** JSON plan = tool + arguments
- **Validation + execution:** `tool_executor` → Product Shell API + UI shell queue
- **Answer:** natural language summary from tool results

---

## One analogy for the jury

> « Atlas, c’est comme un **dispatcher** dans une centrale : il comprend la demande, choisit la **bonne procédure** dans un catalogue, notre **backend** fait le travail technique, et Atlas **reformule** le résultat pour l’utilisateur. »

---

## If they ask: “Why not let GPT do everything?”

> « Parce que le transport doit être **reproductible et testable** : même graphe GTFS, même API, que ce soit l’UI manuelle ou Atlas. L’IA sert à **comprendre le langage** et **choisir l’action**, pas à remplacer le moteur de routage. »

---

## Small correction vs the diagram (if a jury is strict)

The dotted line “OpenAI/Ollama when shortcuts fail” is accurate for **tool selection**. The boxes **`try_ui_settings_intent`** / **`try_deterministic_intent`** run **before** the full intent router on some paths; in production, **`run_planner_turn()`** can also use the **intent router** (`extract_intent_openai` + domain routers) when that mode is enabled. You can say:

> « On a plusieurs niveaux de rapidité : règles fixes, puis routeur d’intentions, puis planificateur LLM si nécessaire. »

That keeps the slide honest without overloading it.

If you want, I can add this as a “Soutenance script” section in `docs/atlas_agent_slide_diagram.md`.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Your mental model is **close**, but one important mix-up: the **domain router is not the local planner**, and **Ollama is not the step after “no match” on shortcuts** in the usual setup.

There are **two modes** in the code. Only one runs per request.

---

## Default mode (most common): `ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER` off

Order in `planner_pipeline.py`:

```
1. Shortcuts / keyword rules     → if match → execute tool
2. OpenAI planner (primary)      → JSON: which tool + args
3. Local Ollama (fallback only)  → only if OpenAI fails or is unavailable
```

So in practice:

| Step | What it is |
|------|------------|
| **Shortcuts** | Fixed rules (`planner_shortcuts.py`) — e.g. “open 3D graph” |
| **OpenAI** | Main brain for normal sentences — `_plan_next_step_openai()` + `_PLANNER_SYSTEM` |
| **Local planner (Ollama)** | **Backup**, not a middle step — used when OpenAI errors or no API key (depending on config) |

**Not:** shortcuts → local planner → OpenAI  
**Yes:** shortcuts → **OpenAI** → (if OpenAI fails) **Ollama**

---

## Optional mode: intent router on (`ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER=1`)

That’s what your diagram describes. Flow in `intent_pipeline.py`:

```
1. try_ui_settings_intent        → UI shortcuts
2. OpenAI intent extractor       → JSON: domain + intent + entities (NOT tool names)
   OR try_deterministic_intent   → if OpenAI fails
3. route_intent()                → central router
4. Domain routers (Python)       → transport / POI / map / 3D
5. routing_decision_to_planner_plan() → map to cspe_* tools
```

Here:

- **Domain routers = normal Python code**, not Ollama.
- OpenAI is used first to **understand** (“route from A to B”), then **rules** pick the tool (`cspe_compute_route`, etc.).
- **Local Ollama is not in this path** for intent routing.

---

## Simple comparison

| | Your diagram (intent router) | Default planner |
|--|------------------------------|-----------------|
| After shortcuts | OpenAI **intent** JSON | OpenAI **tool** JSON |
| Domain routers | Yes (Python) | No |
| Local Ollama | Not in this path | Fallback after OpenAI fails |

---

> « On utilise d’abord des **raccourcis déterministes** pour les commandes simples — pas d’IA, c’est rapide.  
>  
> Ensuite, selon la configuration, soit un **routeur d’intentions** : OpenAI extrait l’intention (transport, POI…), puis du **code métier** choisit l’outil ; soit directement le **planificateur OpenAI**, qui renvoie un JSON avec l’outil `cspe_*` et ses paramètres.  
>  
> Le **planificateur local Ollama**, ce n’est pas une étape entre les deux : c’est un **secours** si OpenAI n’est pas disponible ou échoue.  
>  
> Dans tous les cas, l’IA **choisit l’action** ; c’est **notre backend** qui exécute route, carte et graphe. »

## One-line correction of your question

> « Shortcuts first; if no match, we usually go **straight to the OpenAI planner** (tool JSON). The **domain router** is a **separate optional path** where OpenAI extracts **intent**, then **Python** maps it to tools — that’s **not** the local Ollama planner. Ollama is only a **fallback** after OpenAI. »

If you want one slide: draw **two columns** — “Intent router (optional)” vs “OpenAI planner (default)” — so the jury doesn’t think there are three LLM steps in series.

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

**No — not in the way you’re describing it.**

You do **not** mainly rely on a local router that tries everything first, then fall back to OpenAI when it fails.

---

## Direct answer

| What you thought | What actually happens |
|------------------|------------------------|
| Local router tries first | **Only tiny shortcuts** try first (fixed rules) |
| OpenAI only if local fails | **OpenAI is used for most normal sentences** |
| Local router “understands” language | **Python routers map intent → tool**; they don’t replace OpenAI for NL |

---

## Two modes (ignore Ollama)

### A) Default — intent router **off** (`ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER` default = off)

```
Shortcuts (few fixed phrases)
    ↓ no match
OpenAI planner  ← main path for "route Nation to Orly", etc.
    ↓
Execute tool
```

Most chat goes to **OpenAI**, which returns JSON: tool + arguments.  
There is **no** local domain router in this path.

---

### B) Intent router **on** (your logs show `path=intent_router`)

```
UI shortcuts (very small set)
    ↓ no match
OpenAI intent extractor  ← still OpenAI, but only "domain + intent + entities"
    ↓
Local Python routers   ← map that structure to cspe_* tools
    ↓
Execute tool
```

Here OpenAI still runs **before** the local routers, not after.  
The local part is: “given intent = route, call `cspe_compute_route`” — **rules**, not free-form NL understanding.

If OpenAI intent extraction **fails**, then **`try_deterministic_intent`** (regex/rules) is used as backup — still not “OpenAI as last resort.”

---

## What the “local router” really is

It is **not** a second brain. It is **routing logic in Python**:

- transport → `cspe_compute_route`, `cspe_explore_area`, …
- POI → `cspe_nearby_pois`, …
- map UI → `cspe_transport_action`, …

OpenAI (or shortcuts) supplies **what the user wants**; the router supplies **which tool implements it**.

---

## One sentence for soutenance

> « On utilise d’abord quelques **règles fixes** pour les cas évidents ; pour le reste, **OpenAI comprend la demande** (intention ou choix d’outil), puis du **code local** applique des règles métier pour appeler le bon outil — ce n’est pas l’inverse. »

---

## If they ask: “So do we need OpenAI?”

> « Pour le langage naturel libre, **oui** — sauf les phrases couvertes par les raccourcis. Le routeur local **organise** la décision, il ne **remplace** pas la compréhension du texte. »

Your diagram is fine for **intent-router mode**, but label it clearly: **OpenAI = understanding**, **domain router = execution mapping**, not “local first, AI last.”

---

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
OpenAI outputs StructuredIntent JSON containing domain, intent, and entities. It does not include tool names. The central intent router then routes to the domain router.

The domain router then constructs an ExecutionPlan using actual cspe_* tools. In default planner mode, OpenAI outputs tool calls directly within the _PLANNER_SYSTEM schema. For the intent router path, a sample OpenAI response for a transport query would contain domain "transport", intent "route", and entities mapping origin "Nation" and destination "Aéroport d'Orly".</details></think>

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

**Yes — in intent-router mode, that’s correct.**  
The domain router does **not** read free text again. It reads the **structured JSON from OpenAI** (`domain`, `intent`, `entities`, …) and **Python rules** turn that into a concrete tool like `cspe_compute_route`.

Important nuance: OpenAI does **not** output the tool name in that mode. It outputs **intent**; your code picks the tool.

---

## Intent-router mode (what your diagram shows)

### Step 1 — User says:
> « Show me the route from Nation to Aéroport d’Orly »

### Step 2 — OpenAI outputs (intent JSON, no `cspe_*` tools)

From `intent_extractor.py` → `_INTENT_SYSTEM`:

```json
{
  "domain": "transport",
  "intent": "route",
  "entities": {
    "station": null,
    "origin": "Nation",
    "destination": "Aéroport d'Orly",
    "line": null,
    "mode": "metro",
    "poi_category": null,
    "place": null
  },
  "ui_action": true,
  "response_type": "text_and_ui",
  "confidence": 0.92,
  "assumptions": [],
  "normalized_query": "route from Nation to Aéroport d'Orly"
}
```

OpenAI answers: *“This is a transport route request from Nation to Orly, and the user wants the map updated.”*  
It does **not** say `cspe_compute_route`.

### Step 3 — Local router decides the tool (Python)

`route_intent()` → `route_transport()` in `domain_routers.py` sees `intent == "route"` and builds:

```json
{
  "tool": "cspe_compute_route",
  "arguments": {
    "from_query": "Nation",
    "to_query": "Aéroport d'Orly",
    "mode": "metro",
    "routing_scope": "station",
    "sync_ui": true
  }
}
```

That matches your logs:  
`path=intent_router` … `tool='cspe_compute_route'` … `model=openai_intent`

### Step 4 — `tool_executor` runs that tool on the Product Shell.

---

## Another example — POIs

**User:** « Show POIs around République »

**OpenAI intent JSON:**
```json
{
  "domain": "poi",
  "intent": "explore_area",
  "entities": {
    "station": "République",
    "origin": null,
    "destination": null,
    "mode": "metro",
    "poi_category": "all",
    "place": null
  },
  "ui_action": true,
  "response_type": "text_and_ui",
  "confidence": 0.9,
  "assumptions": [],
  "normalized_query": "POIs around République"
}
```

**Local POI router → tool:**
```json
{
  "tool": "cspe_nearby_pois",
  "arguments": {
    "query": "République",
    "categories": ["all"],
    "radius_m": 500,
    "sync_ui": true,
    "mode": "metro",
    "limit": 30
  }
}
```

---

## Alternative mode — OpenAI picks the tool directly

When intent router is **off**, OpenAI skips the intent layer and returns a **planner JSON** with tools directly (`agent_planner.py` → `_PLANNER_SYSTEM`):

**User:** same route question

**OpenAI planner JSON:**
```json
{
  "status": "continue",
  "steps": [
    {
      "tool": "cspe_compute_route",
      "arguments": {
        "from_query": "Nation",
        "to_query": "Aéroport d'Orly",
        "mode": "all",
        "sync_ui": true
      },
      "reason": "User asked for a route between two stations"
    }
  ],
  "tool_name": null,
  "args": {},
  "clarifying_question": "",
  "final_summary": "",
  "topic": "transport"
}
```

Here there is **no domain router step** — the model names the tool itself.

---

## Summary table

| | Intent router ON | Intent router OFF |
|--|------------------|-------------------|
| **OpenAI outputs** | Intent JSON (domain, intent, entities) | Planner JSON (`tool` + `arguments`) |
| **Who picks the tool?** | Python domain router | OpenAI directly |
| **Example tool** | Router maps `route` → `cspe_compute_route` | Model returns `cspe_compute_route` |

---

## One sentence for soutenance

> « OpenAI extrait **l’intention structurée** ; nos **routeurs Python** transforment ça en **outil CSPE** (`cspe_compute_route`, `cspe_nearby_pois`, …) avec des règles métier fiables. »

So: **yes, the router uses OpenAI’s structured output — but OpenAI gives intent, not the final tool name** (in intent-router mode).

**Intent router is ON** in your current setup.

Three pieces of evidence:

1. **Your `.env`** (line 15):
   ```
   ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER=1
   ```

2. **`run_web_app.ps1`** loads that file at startup (`Import-RepoDotEnv`), so Atlas sees it when you run the app.

3. **Your activity logs** confirm it’s active:
   - `path=intent_router`
   - `plan_source=intent_router`
   - `model=openai_intent`
   - `openai_planner_used=False`

---

**Code default vs your config**

In `planner_config.py`, the default is **off** if the env var is missing:

```121:128:src/work/atlas/src/atlas_client/core/planner_config.py
def intent_router_enabled() -> bool:
    """When true, use structured intent routing instead of OpenAI tool selection."""
    return (os.getenv("ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER") or "0").strip().lower() in (
        "1",
        "true",
        "yes",
        "on",
    )
```

You explicitly turned it on with `ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER=1`.

---

**What that means right now**

| Step | What runs |
|------|-----------|
| 1 | OpenAI intent extractor → JSON (`domain`, `intent`, `entities`) |
| 2 | Python domain routers → pick `cspe_*` tool |
| 3 | Tool executor → Product Shell |

The direct OpenAI tool planner (`_plan_next_step_openai`) is **not** the primary path while this flag is on.

To switch back to direct tool planning, set `ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER=0` (or remove the line) and restart the app.

Created **`docs/atlas_planner_direct_openai_diagram.md`**.

It mirrors your slide layout but:

- **Removed** StructuredIntent, `route_intent()`, domain routers, and `routing_decision_to_planner_plan()`
- **Shows** OpenAI choosing the tool directly → planner JSON → validate → `tool_executor`
- **No mention** of Ollama or local models

Flow in the diagram:

1. `try_ui_settings_intent` → match → tool executor  
2. `try_deterministic_intent` → match → tool executor  
3. **OpenAI planner** → JSON with `steps[].tool` + `arguments`  
4. `validate_and_enrich_plan()`  
5. `tool_executor` → Product Shell  

It also includes a concrete JSON example for a Nation → Orly route and a one-line French summary for your soutenance.

**Note:** Your live app still has `ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER=1` in `.env`, so production uses the domain-router path. This doc describes the **direct OpenAI planner** model for presentation — set `ATLAS_INTENT_ROUTER=0` if you want the running app to match the diagram.

```json
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 728,
            "text": "---"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 729
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 730,
            "text": "## 13. Memory and context"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 731
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 732,
            "text": "### Two memory systems (not synced)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 733
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 734,
            "text": "| System | Storage | Access |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 735,
            "text": "|--------|---------|--------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 736,
            "text": "| **Product memory** | &#96;data/product_memory.sqlite&#96; | &#96;/api/memory/*&#96;, Memory mode UI |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 737,
            "text": "| **Atlas agent memory** | Atlas SQLite (under &#96;src/work/atlas/data/&#96;) | &#96;memory_*&#96; tools |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 738
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 739,
            "text": "### Agent world state (&#96;agent_store.py&#96;)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 740
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 741,
            "text": "Patches via:"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 742
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 743,
            "text": "- Exploration: &#96;_store_exploration_snapshot()&#96; → &#96;transport.last_exploration&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 744,
            "text": "- Browser: &#96;AgentContextSync&#96; → &#96;ui_mode&#96;, &#96;transport.graph_mode&#96;, paths"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 745,
            "text": "- Shell commands: route views, mode changes"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 746
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 747,
            "text": "### Planner context consumption"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 748
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 749,
            "text": "- **&#96;cspe_get_current_context&#96;** / **&#96;agent_fetch_context&#96;** → full JSON"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 750,
            "text": "- Deictic queries (\"near here\"): **&#96;query_from_agent_context()&#96;** in &#96;transport_exploration.py&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 751,
            "text": "- Selected station from last exploration or UI patch"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 752
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 753,
            "text": "### Todos / reminders"
          }
        ],

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "lineNumber": 556,
            "text": "Default mode. Flat map, stops/stations, route polylines, exploration markers."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 557
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 558,
            "text": "## Network 3D map mode (&#96;network_3d&#96;)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 559
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 560,
            "text": "**Still Mapbox** — pitched camera and 3D buildings where available. **Not** the GraphXR network graph."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 561
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 562,
            "text": "## Overlays"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 563
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 564,
            "text": "| Overlay | Mechanism |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 565,
            "text": "|---------|-----------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 566,
            "text": "| **Route** | Path IDs in map request or &#96;POST /transport/map/route-overlay&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 567,
            "text": "| **Exploration** | &#96;POST /transport/map/exploration-overlay&#96; + iframe &#96;postMessage&#96; (&#96;mapExplorationBridge.ts&#96;) |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 568,
            "text": "| **Selection** | Selected stop/station ID in map body |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 569
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 570,
            "text": "Incremental overlays avoid full map rebuild when possible."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 571
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 572,
            "text": "## Frontend panels / UI"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 573
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 574,
            "text": "Floating HUD: left stack (controls), bottom dock (route/search), Atlas rail (right). **F** focus mode hides HUD; **graph3d** mode hides almost everything except “← Map” exit."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 575
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 576,
            "text": "## GraphXR 3D/VR viewer"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 577
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 578,
            "text": "- Path: &#96;viewers/graphxr/&#96; — Next.js + Babylon.js"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 579,
            "text": "- URL: &#96;http://127.0.0.1:3000/viewer?session=…\u0026api=…\u0026sync=…\u0026embedded=1&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 580,
            "text": "- Loads project JSON from &#96;GET /api/transport/graph3d/session/{id}&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 581,
            "text": "- **Live sync:** polls &#96;GET /api/transport/graph3d/sync/{client_id}&#96; every ~900 ms"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 582,
            "text": "- **WebXR:** &#96;GraphSceneXR.tsx&#96; for headset; Quest needs HTTPS (&#96;-QuestVR&#96;)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 583
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 584,
            "text": "## Mapbox 3D vs GraphXR 3D/VR (critical distinction)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 585
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 586,
            "text": "| | Mapbox &#96;network_3d&#96; | GraphXR &#96;graph3d&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 587,
            "text": "|--|---------------------|-------------------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 588,
            "text": "| **What it shows** | Real geography, streets, buildings | Abstract **network graph** (nodes = stops/stations) |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 589,
            "text": "| **Technology** | Mapbox GL HTML | Babylon.js + WebXR |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 590,
            "text": "| **Use case** | Geographic context | Network topology, VR immersion |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 591,
            "text": "| **Route highlight** | Polyline on map | Orange nodes/edges in graph |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 592
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 593,
            "text": "## Caching"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 594
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 595,
            "text": "| Cache | Location | TTL / size |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 596,
            "text": "|-------|----------|------------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 597,
            "text": "| Graph bundle | Memory after first load | Process lifetime |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 598,
            "text": "| Map HTML | Memory (24 entries) + disk &#96;map_html_cache/&#96; | Per fingerprint |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 599,
            "text": "| Graph3d session | In-memory &#96;_GRAPH3D_SESSIONS&#96; | 30 minutes |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 600,
            "text": "| Graph3d sync registry | In-memory &#96;_GRAPH3D_SYNC&#96; | 1 hour |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 601,
            "text": "| POI BallTree | Loaded once from pickle/npz | Process lifetime |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 602
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 603,
            "text": "---"
          }
        ],
        "range": {
          "endPosition": {
            "line": 604
          },
          "startPosition": {
            "line": 555
          }
        },
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\docs\\full_project_explanation_for_presentation.md",
        "signatures": {}
      },
      "score": 0.48956969380378723

      "codeBlock": {
        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "lineNumber": 724,
            "text": "| **Warmup thread** | First route/map faster after startup |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 725,
            "text": "| **Transport-only UI scope** | Focused product; other modes removed from current tree |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 726
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 727,
            "text": "---"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 728
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 729,
            "text": "# 13. Implemented features"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 730
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 731,
            "text": "| Feature | Status | Main files | Short explanation |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 732,
            "text": "|---------|--------|------------|-------------------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 733,
            "text": "| GTFS graph bundle | Implemented | &#96;graph_loader.py&#96;, &#96;cache_bundle.py&#96;, &#96;rebuild_routing_bundle.py&#96; | Offline multimodal network |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 734,
            "text": "| Stop/station search | Implemented | &#96;queries.py&#96;, &#96;transport_engine.py&#96; | Autocomplete with station grouping |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 735,
            "text": "| Shortest-path routing | Implemented | &#96;queries.py&#96;, &#96;transport_engine.py&#96; | Hop-based NetworkX paths + summaries |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 736,

          },

          },

          {
            "lineNumber": 129,
            "text": "| **Processing** | &#96;POST /api/transport/graph3d/sync&#96; → session JSON built from graph + route highlight → embedded iframe &#96;viewers/graphxr&#96; with &#96;embedded=1&#96; |"
          },
          {

          },

            "text": "**Status:** **Implemented** (embedded same-page mode; GraphXR dev server on :3000)."

          {
            "lineNumber": 133
          },
          {

            "text": "| **Processing** | &#96;POST /api/atlas/input-mode&#96; &#96;{mode:\"voice\"}&#96; → Atlas orchestrator (OpenAI Realtime, per architecture) → same tools as text |"

            "lineNumber": 141
          },

          },

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "lineNumber": 690,
            "text": "## Example C — Manual route + 3D visualization"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 691
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 692,
            "text": "| Step | Layer | Detail |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 693,
            "text": "|------|-------|--------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 694,
            "text": "| 1 | User | Enters start/end in route dock, clicks Compute |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 695,
            "text": "| 2 | Frontend | &#96;POST /api/transport/route&#96; directly |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 696,
            "text": "| 3 | Backend | Same &#96;compute_route()&#96; as Atlas path |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 697,
            "text": "| 4 | Result | Path IDs stored in Zustand |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 698,
            "text": "| 5 | Viz | Map shows route on Mapbox iframe |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 699,
            "text": "| 6 | User | Clicks “3D/VR graph” |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 700,
            "text": "| 7 | Frontend | &#96;setTransportViz(\"graph3d\")&#96; → &#96;pushGraph3dViewSync(true)&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 701,
            "text": "| 8 | Backend | New graph3d session with route nodes highlighted orange |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 702,
            "text": "| 9 | Viz | Full-screen GraphXR iframe; optional VR button |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 703
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 704,
            "text": "---"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 705
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 706,
            "text": "# 12. Important technical decisions"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 707
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 708,
            "text": "| Decision | Why |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 709,
            "text": "|----------|-----|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 710,
            "text": "| **FastAPI product shell (single :8787)** | One BFF for UI + Atlas tools; replaces older split APIs |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 711,
            "text": "| **React + Vite frontend** | Modern SPA, fast dev, iframe-friendly for map/GraphXR |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 712,
            "text": "| **Mapbox server-side HTML** | Keeps token secret; consistent rendering; works in iframe |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 713,
            "text": "| **NetworkX for graphs** | Mature graph library; GTFS → graph is natural fit |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 714,
            "text": "| **Ride + transfer edge model** | Separates in-vehicle movement from interchange realism |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 715,
            "text": "| **Rich edge attributes (time, cost, distance)** | Enables realistic summaries and future weighted routing |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 716,
            "text": "| **Hop routing (current)** | Simpler path selection today; weights stored but not used in &#96;shortest_path()&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 717,
            "text": "| **Shell command queue** | Decouples Atlas tools from React; single consumer applies UI deltas |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 718,
            "text": "| **GraphXR separate app** | Isolates WebXR/Babylon weight from main React bundle |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 719,
            "text": "| **Embedded GraphXR iframe** | Same-page immersive UX without popup blockers |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 720,
            "text": "| **OpenAI as planner/realtime** | Strong NLU and voice without training custom models |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 721,
            "text": "| **Optional Ollama local planner** | Reduce latency/cost for tool selection; OpenAI still responds |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 722,
            "text": "| **Station layer on top of stop graph** | GTFS is stop-level; users think in stations |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 723,
            "text": "| **IDFM for enrichment only** | Routing stays offline/reproducible; live API for hours/accessibility |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 724,
            "text": "| **Warmup thread** | First route/map faster after startup |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 725,
            "text": "| **Transport-only UI scope** | Focused product; other modes removed from current tree |"
          }
        ],
        "range": {
          "endPosition": {
            "line": 725
          },
          "startPosition": {
            "line": 689
          }
        },
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\docs\\full_project_explanation_for_presentation.md",
        "signatures": {}

        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "lineNumber": 659,
            "text": "### Inputs (&#96;TransportMapRequest&#96;)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 660
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 661,
            "text": "- &#96;mode&#96;, &#96;use_lcc&#96;, &#96;viz_mode&#96; (geographic vs network_3d pitched)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 662,
            "text": "- &#96;path_stop_ids&#96;, &#96;path_station_ids&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 663,
            "text": "- &#96;selected_stop_id&#96;, &#96;selected_station_id&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 664,
            "text": "- &#96;exploration_overlay&#96; (center, radius, nearby_stops/pois)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 665,
            "text": "- &#96;poi_radius_m&#96;, &#96;poi_limit&#96;, &#96;poi_category_key&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 666
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 667,
            "text": "### Mapbox HTML (&#96;plot_mapbox.py&#96;)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 668
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 669,
            "text": "- Embeds **&#96;map_payload&#96;** JSON in &#96;\u003cscript\u003e&#96; (network GeoJSON, paths, stations, exploration layers, token)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 670,
            "text": "- Loads Mapbox GL JS v3.4 from CDN"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 671,
            "text": "- Layers: network lines, route path, stations, transfers, exploration stop/POI circles"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 672,
            "text": "- **Paris/IDF mask** from &#96;paris_mask.build_paris_mask_payload()&#96; when GeoJSON exists"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 673,
            "text": "- Exploration center sets map center as **&#96;{lon, lat}&#96;** object (required by map init JS)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 674
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 675,
            "text": "### Caching"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 676
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 677,
            "text": "- In-memory cache keyed by request parameters + exploration overlay string"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 678,
            "text": "- Disk cache under &#96;data/derived/product_shell/map_html_cache/&#96; for static maps (disabled when exploration overlay present)"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 679
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 680,
            "text": "### Frontend map update flow"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 681
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 682,
            "text": "1. Shell command sets exploration + &#96;exploration_map&#96; action"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 683,
            "text": "2. &#96;TransportMode&#96; applies patches, calls **&#96;refreshMap()&#96;**"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 684,
            "text": "3. Map HTML blob loaded in iframe"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 685,
            "text": "4. Logs: &#96;[Exploration] map_render ...&#96; in &#96;activity_compact.log&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 686
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 687,
            "text": "### Key functions"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 688
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 689,
            "text": "| Function | File |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 690,
            "text": "|----------|------|"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 691,
            "text": "| &#96;render_transport_map_html&#96; | &#96;transport_engine.py&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 692,
            "text": "| &#96;render_mapbox_gl_html&#96; | &#96;plot_mapbox.py&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 693,
            "text": "| &#96;_exploration_geojson&#96; | &#96;plot_mapbox.py&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 694,
            "text": "| &#96;build_paris_mask_payload&#96; | &#96;paris_mask.py&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 695,
            "text": "| &#96;load_line_geometries&#96; | &#96;plot_mapbox.py&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 696,
            "text": "| &#96;load_render_graph&#96; | &#96;plot_mapbox.py&#96; |"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 697
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 698,
            "text": "---"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 699
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 700,
            "text": "## 12. 3D graph / immersive visualization"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 701
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 702,
            "text": "### Session flow"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 703
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 704,
            "text": "1. **&#96;POST /api/transport/graph3d/session&#96;** → &#96;transport_engine.create_graph3d_session()&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 705,
            "text": "2. Builds graph payload (nodes, links, route highlight) for mode/LCC/path"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 706,
            "text": "3. Returns &#96;session_id&#96;, metadata"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 707,
            "text": "4. Frontend opens: &#96;{GRAPHXR_BASE}/viewer?session={id}\u0026api={PRODUCT_SHELL_URL}&#96;"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 708,
            "text": "5. GraphXR **&#96;GET /api/transport/graph3d/session/{session_id}&#96;** fetches JSON"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 709
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 710,
            "text": "### Atlas tool"
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 711
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 712,
            "text": "**&#96;cspe_open_graph3d&#96;** — opens viewer URL in browser; uses &#96;VITE_GRAPHXR_VIEWER_URL&#96; or &#96;CSPE_FRONTEND_URL&#96; defaults."
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 713
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 714,
            "text": "### Viewer stack"

            "lineNumber": 715
          },
          {

          }
```

_**Agent (composer-2.5)**_

Here is a clear way to explain **3D/VR** in your soutenance — simple on the surface, but with enough technical detail if the jury asks follow-ups.

---

## The one sentence (say this first)

> « For the **2D map**, we use Mapbox. For **3D/VR**, we reuse a **GraphXR viewer** from a previous project and **connect it to our transport graph** so the user can explore the network in 3D or in a VR headset, with the **current route highlighted**. »

That is honest: you did not build Babylon.js from scratch — you **integrated** an existing viewer with CSPE.

---

## Three visualization modes (important distinction)

Your app has **three** “3D-ish” things. Only one is GraphXR/VR:

| Mode | What the user sees | Technology |
|------|-------------------|------------|
| **Geographic** | Flat Paris map, stops, routes | Mapbox (server-generated HTML) |
| **3D map** (`network_3d`) | Same map, tilted camera + 3D buildings | Still **Mapbox** — not VR |
| **3D/VR graph** (`graph3d`) | Abstract **network graph** (nodes = stops/stations, edges = links) | **GraphXR** (Next.js + Babylon.js + WebXR) |

If someone asks “is your 3D the map in VR?” — answer: **No.** Mapbox 3D is geographic. GraphXR is a **topology graph** you can walk through in VR.

---

## What GraphXR is (and what you reused)

- **GraphXR** lives in `viewers/graphxr/` — a separate **Next.js app** on port **3000**.
- It comes from last year’s prototype (**A25-iviz-main**), now maintained as `viewers/graphxr/`.
- It uses **Babylon.js** to render nodes/edges in 3D.
- **WebXR** (`GraphSceneXR.tsx`) lets a **Meta Quest** (or other WebXR browser) enter immersive VR.

**Your CSPE contribution** is not “we invented a 3D engine”, but:

1. Export the **same GTFS routing graph** CSPE already uses into a **JSON session** the viewer understands.
2. **Highlight the computed route** (orange nodes/edges).
3. **Embed** the viewer in the main app (iframe, fullscreen).
4. **Live sync** when the user changes route, mode, or selection.
5. **Quest support** via HTTPS proxy (`run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR`).

That is a valid integration story for a master’s project.

---

## How it works — step by step

### 1. User opens 3D/VR

- Button **“3D/VR graph”** in `TransportMode.tsx`, or Atlas tool `cspe_open_graph3d` / shell command `transport_graph3d_sync`.
- Frontend switches `transportViz` to `"graph3d"` → fullscreen iframe, Atlas rail hidden.

### 2. Frontend sends current transport state to the backend

`graph3dSync.ts` calls:

```
POST /api/transport/graph3d/sync
```

With things like:

- graph mode (metro / rail / …)
- LCC on/off
- current route (`path_stop_ids` or `path_station_ids`)
- selected stop/station
- a **fingerprint** of the whole view (so the backend knows when something changed)

### 3. Backend builds a “graph session”

In `transport_engine.py`, `create_graph3d_session()`:

1. Loads the **same NetworkX graph** used for routing (`graph_bundle.pkl`).
2. Converts it to **GraphProject JSON**:
   - **nodes**: id, label, x/y/z position, color by transport mode
   - **edges**: source, target, weight, color
3. Applies **highlights**:
   - Route nodes/edges → orange `#f97316`, thicker edges
   - Selected stop → red
4. Stores the JSON in memory with a **session id** (TTL ~30 min).

The viewer does **not** read GTFS files. It only reads this prepared JSON.

### 4. Frontend opens GraphXR in an iframe

URL shape:

```
http://127.0.0.1:3000/viewer?session=<id>&api=http://127.0.0.1:8787&sync=<client_id>&embedded=1
```

- `session` → which graph snapshot to load  
- `api` → Product Shell base URL  
- `sync` → client id for live updates  
- `embedded=1` → hide GraphXR chrome (CSPE controls the page)

### 5. GraphXR loads and renders

`ViewerClient.tsx`:

1. `GET /api/transport/graph3d/session/{session_id}` → full graph JSON  
2. `GraphSceneWeb.tsx` → desktop 3D (mouse orbit, zoom)  
3. Optional **VR button** → `GraphSceneXR.tsx` → WebXR session in the headset  

Rendering: Babylon.js draws spheres/cylinders for nodes/edges (`GraphRenderer`).

### 6. Live sync (route changes while viewer is open)

Two sides push/pull:

- **CSPE frontend**: when route/mode/selection changes, calls `pushGraph3dViewSync()` again → new session + new fingerprint.
- **GraphXR viewer**: every **~900 ms** polls  
  `GET /api/transport/graph3d/sync/{client_id}?fingerprint=...`  
  If fingerprint changed → loads the **new session id** and refreshes the graph.

So if Atlas computes a new route on the map, the 3D graph can update without closing VR.

---

## VR specifically (Meta Quest)

- WebXR needs **HTTPS** on Quest (not plain `http://127.0.0.1`).
- `.\run_web_app.ps1 -QuestVR` starts:
  - GraphXR on `:3000`
  - Product Shell on `:8787`
  - Vite on `:5173`
  - An **HTTPS proxy** (often + ngrok) so the headset has one secure URL.
- In the viewer, user clicks the VR/glasses control → Babylon enters **immersive VR** → user moves in the graph with controllers (`GraphSceneXR.tsx`, Oculus Touch support).

---

## Simple diagram you can draw on a slide

```
User (browser or Quest)
    │
    ▼
CSPE React (:5173)  ──POST graph3d/sync──►  Product Shell (:8787)
    │                                              │
    │ iframe                                       │ create_graph3d_session()
    ▼                                              │ (GTFS graph → JSON + route highlight)
GraphXR (:3000)  ◄──GET session/{id}──────────────┘
    │
    ├── GraphSceneWeb  (3D on screen)
    └── GraphSceneXR   (WebXR in headset)
         poll sync every 900ms ◄──► Product Shell
```

---

## What to say if they ask “did you build the 3D viewer?”

> « The **3D/VR engine** is based on **GraphXR**, a viewer from a prior academic project (Babylon.js + WebXR). Our work was to **integrate it with CSPE**: export the transport graph from our routing backend, highlight routes and selections, embed it in the product UI, and support **live synchronization** and **Meta Quest** via WebXR. The **routing and data** are ours; the **rendering framework** is reused. »

That is accurate and defensible.

---

## Technical details worth knowing (jury questions)

**Q: Where do node positions come from?**  
From stop coordinates in the graph bundle, scaled into 3D space. Modes can be **layered on the Y axis** (metro on one layer, rail on another) so the graph is readable.

**Q: How is the route shown in 3D?**  
Same path IDs as the 2D map. Backend marks nodes/edges with `is_route: true` and orange color before sending JSON.

**Q: Is 3D routing different from 2D?**  
No — same graph, same path. Only the **visualization** changes.

**Q: Why a separate app on port 3000?**  
WebXR + Babylon is heavy. Keeping GraphXR separate avoids bloating the main Vite bundle and isolates VR lifecycle.

**Q: Limitations?**  
- Sessions expire (~30 min in memory).  
- Large graphs (e.g. full bus) can be slow.  
- Routing is still **hop-based**, not time-optimal — same limitation as the 2D map.

---

**Titre:** Visualisation 3D / VR du réseau de transport

**Texte:**
- Carte 2D = Mapbox · Graphe 3D/VR = GraphXR (Babylon.js + WebXR)
- Le backend CSPE convertit le graphe GTFS en JSON de session
- Le trajet calculé est surligné en orange
- Le viewer est intégré en iframe ; synchronisation live par empreinte (fingerprint)
- Mode Quest : proxy HTTPS + WebXR
